Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga women have bucked the revolving door trend in new era: 'We recruit uniquely'
Gonzaga.summary:
In a time when a premium is placed on player retention and roster rebuilding, we give you the antithesis: Gonzaga women’s basketball.

At the same time college basketball seems to shift with each change in wind direction, Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier longs for the old days. Back when building a roster began and ended with high school freshmen.

COVID-19 and the recent 5-for-5 eligibility change has thrown wrenches into the formula in which Gonzaga was built on.

Gonzaga desires that its foundation includes high school players. When the program started making a name for itself in the mid -2000s, the Zags were signing high school players. Before Fortier and continuing during her watch, Gonzaga has followed that formula. Recruit and sign high school athletes, take time to develop them and ultimately reap the benefits.

“We recruit uniquely,” Fortier said. “We’ve never been the group that just amasses talent. We’ve tried to find the right pieces to fit in together. And there is some movement … you can only control so much of that. But we take good care of them. We surround them with people you want to hang out with.”

Fortier has seen it up close for two decades. She’s beginning her 13th season as the Zags’ head coach and 20th overall.

It’s not a coincidence that many programs across the nation have had to eschew the once -traditional means of developing and sustaining their teams – through the signing and development of high school players – for quick fixes brought on by graduation or losses in the transfer portal – in hopes of remaining competitive and not falling behind the winning curve.

Gonzaga has stayed ahead of the curve.

Go back two decades when Gonzaga came on the mid-major scene and started giving teams from power conferences all they could handle. The Bulldogs had an occasional transfer back then, but the bedrock of their success has always been homegrown talent.

Along came COVID-19 followed by name, image and likeness – all of which threw recruiting cycles out of whack. Now comes the initiation of the 5-in-5 eligibility model.

“We used to write out on a whiteboard four or five seasons (rosters) and what that looks like,” assistant coach Craig Fortier said.

Gonzaga doesn’t do that anymore.

“What Lisa promotes is ‘Let’s bring in great people that can get better,’ ” Craig said. “And if we can keep them, then they will get better. We’re always going to be excited to have them as long as we can have them. We never want to have somebody that we’re kind of happy when they head out the door.”

Four of five starters on Gonzaga’s Super Seniors team in 2023-24 were prized high school recruits, developed over four or five years. Interestingly, though, it created some roster consternation. The last two recruiting classes have brought in four freshmen, one of whom transferred out this spring. The 2026-27 roster features one freshman. And the Zags have one commitment for the 2027 class.

How many more players Gonzaga will need to bring in next year depends on how many seniors exercise a fifth-year option created with the new eligibility format.

Seniors Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso and McKynnlie Dalan – each of whom transferred to Gonzaga – may opt to play another year, transfer for their final season or walk away from basketball.

This year’s roster features six juniors who could play three more seasons including this season. Junior Lauren Whittaker, who was listed on the roster as a redshirt freshman a year ago, is now listed as a junior to be in compliance with the new eligibility rule.

Seven of Gonzaga’s 13 players are transfers. No previous roster has had more transfers.

Thankfully most of Gonzaga’s transfers over the years have had at least two years of eligibility and in some cases three and maybe four.

Of the current group of transfers, Dalan could end up playing four at Gonzaga after spending her freshman season at the University of Minnesota. Former Mead three-sport standout Teryn Gardner could spend four years with the Zags.

Fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt, who hopes a temporary injunction granting her another year eligibility holds up this season, transferred from UConn to Gonzaga two years ago.

This year’s transfers – junior guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) – could spend three seasons at Gonzaga.

“So they’ve started to become our guys in our culture because we’ve had them for a while,” Craig Fortier said. “No matter if they’re a transfer or a freshman, the pattern is always going to be development. The more time you get with them, the better generally you’re gonna do. But we’re also trying to be effective and efficient with whatever amount of time we have with them in getting people up to speed with how we want to play and how we think we can help them be the best versions of themselves. That’s always evolving.”

Technically, the Zags have two scholarships available by NCAA rule. But Gonzaga has never had 15 on scholarship at one time.

Gonzaga has a commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Aylah Cornwall, who will sign during the early signing period in November. She will essentially fill Bettencourt’s scholarship.

Lisa Fortier says she and her staff continue to recruit for the class of 2027. That’s largely because it’s not known who will exercise a fifth-year option or perhaps transfer. Fortier always wants to have a scholarship in her back pocket.

“We aren’t done with (the 2027 class) yet,” Fortier said. “Most coaches right now are not just taking any high school kid. They have to be a really good fit or a really talented player.”

Gonzaga coaches have been out and about recruiting this fall. The Zags just offered AnnaClaire Bugbee, a 6-2 forward from Mandan, North Dakota, a position in the class of 2028. Bugbee posted a photo of herself with Gonzaga’s coaches on social media recently.

Fortier and her staff are recruiting players for 2028 and 2029.

“We’re recruiting all the time – it never stops,” Fortier said. “Our best players were high school recruits. They are homegrown. That’s a recruiting model we’re comfortable with. It’s hard to place a value on those program kids. You can point to programs like ours where you grow them up, take good care of them and you coach them well. And when they stay they’ll give everything. That’s the kind of people you want on your team – as many of them as you can.”

Gonzaga.title: Loaded Gonzaga women will be team to beat in rebuilt Pac-12
Gonzaga.summary:
The Gonzaga women’s basketball team should discover that many hands make lighter work this season.

Like 10 sets of hands – and maybe a couple more sets depending on the impact of transfers and a freshman.

All five starters return from a team that finished 24-10 and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

Truth is the Bulldogs have seven players capable of starting. And the other three will likely give coach Lisa Fortier pause when it comes to doling out playing time.

The Zags’ abundance of talent begins with 6-foot-3 forward Lauren Whittaker, who broke onto the scene last year as a redshirt freshman and was a force that West Coast Conference teams couldn’t contain. She was named the WCC Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year.

Whittaker is listed as a junior on this year’s roster. Gonzaga is being compliant with the NCAA’s new eligibility rules. Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and used a medical waiver, can play three more years.

She led the Zags with 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game less than a year after having knee surgery. There’s no telling what Whittaker can do with a second year of strength added to her knee.

“It’s been so nice not to rehab anything,” Whittaker said. “I’ve gotten to work a lot on my fitness and stamina. I didn’t really get a summer workout session (last year) because I was just rehabbing the whole time.”

Floating on the perimeter and causing opponents frustration is junior guard Allie Turner, who will start for a third straight season.

An All-WCC first-team selection, Turner was the second-leading 3-point shooter in the nation last season and key to Gonzaga finishing as the top 3-point shooting team, a spot ahead of powerhouse UConn. Turner shot 47.1%, making 89 of 189. The Zags converted 39.2% (244 of 623).

Turner averaged 14.8 points, second best, and 3.5 assists per game.

It was thought Gonzaga would need to replace just one starter. But guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring, has been granted a fifth season through the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model. Bettencourt and 70 other player plaintiffs in the California-based Glancey vs. NCAA lawsuit were granted a preliminary injunction by a California Superior Court judge. She’s still potentially awaiting final clearance from the courts.

A transfer from UConn, Bettencourt, one of Gonzaga’s best defensive players, averaged 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game.

Bettencourt became a strong voice among teammates last season. That should continue this season. She’ll get some assistance from Whittaker and Turner.

The Zags’ other two returning starters, seniors Taylor Smith (forward) and Zeryia Aokuso (guard), had flashes of brilliance last season. Smith should be much more effective and dangerous teaming with Whittaker in the high-low sets, and watch for Aokuso to play the point at times and create offense with her ability to get to the rim.

Forward Jaiden Haile, who was named the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year as a freshman last year, and junior guard Teryn Gardner played key roles off the bench. They would start for many teams, and don’t be surprised if either steps into a starting role at some point this year.

Senior forward McKynnlie Dalan, junior guard Christabel Osarobo and sophomore Julia Wilson round out the 10 returners. They will be fighting for minutes off the bench.

Joining the Zags are junior transfer guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) and freshman forward Abby Lusk, from Pocatello, Idaho. All three had solid minutes at FanFest.

“We have players who can make plays, who can make shots, who can rebound,” Fortier said. “We’re going to be able to play a lot of them and a lot of them are gonna be able to make an impact.”

With a team loaded with experience, preseason practices have allowed the Zags to pick up where they left off.

“We’re still gonna play with two forwards, we’re still gonna run the floor, we’re still gonna shoot a bunch of 3s,” Fortier said. “But within that context it does afford us an opportunity to wiggle a little bit and tinker.”

Gonzaga won’t have any difficulty scoring, and the Zags will look to push the pace whenever they can. But they must cut down on turnovers and improve defensively.

“Defensively we can be a lot better,” Turner said, pointing the finger squarely at herself.

The Zags were ranked 49th by Bart Torvik, whose analytical data is similar to the KenPom rankings in men’s basketball. No other non-Power Four school was represented in Torvik’s top 50.

Gonzaga is heavily favored to win the Pac-12 Conference in its first year in the rebuilt league.

It’s likely just the Pac-12 Tournament winner will earn a berth to the NCAA Tournament. The conference doesn’t have the credentials that the men’s teams have at this point.

The Zags don’t want to just get to the NCAA Tournament, though. They want to do something no other Gonzaga team has done – get to the Elite Eight, if not further.

“Win the conference tournament, make it to postseason and then hopefully get further than a game there this year,” Turner said.

Said Whittaker: “Everyone got a taste of what it’s like to be at the (NCAA) Tournament and everyone wants more. So it’s just elevating from what we had last year. We’ve built that foundation. No excuses. We’ve been together for a year.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Gonzaga.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women picked to win new Pac-12; WSU selected sixth | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
With five starters and five other returners, it is no surprise that the Gonzaga women’s basketball team was tapped to win the Pac-12 Conference championship in a media poll released Thursday.

The Bulldogs’ top seven scorers return from a team that finished 24-10 and won the West Coast Conference title in its final season in the league.

Oregon State was picked to finish second in the remodeled conference. The Beavers may have been picked second based on their reputation and penchant for postseason success. In the final year of the original Pac-12 (2023-24), they advanced to the Elite Eight.

San Diego State, which won the Mountain West championship last year, was picked third followed by Colorado State, Boise State, Washington State, Fresno State, Texas State and Utah State.

Gonzaga received 16 of 19 first-place votes. Oregon State received one and San Diego State received two.

Colorado State won the MWC Tournament last year and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

WSU returns six players who started at various times. The Cougars have much to prove after stumbling to a 9-25 record last year.

ESPN released its preseason bracketology compiled by Charlie Creme on Monday. Gonzaga is picked as the automatic qualifier from the Pac-12 as a 10 seed. Oregon State and San Diego State are picked in the new 76-team field to play play-in games.

Players to watch

The Pac-12 also released its Preseason Impact List.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker, the WCC Player and Freshman of the Year last season, and junior guard Allie Turner, an All-WCC first-team selection a year ago, were two of 18 players named. Each school was allowed to nominate two players.

Named from WSU are seniors Alex Covill (post) and Eleonora Villa (guard), an All-WCC second-team pick last year.

Former WSU guard Jenna Villa and point guard Kennedie Shuler were selected from Oregon State. Shuler was the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and Villa was a first-team selection.

Add to the list

Gonzaga’s Whittaker was named to two more watch lists.

Whittaker, from Christchurch, New Zealand, is on the Naismith Trophy Women’s College Player of the Year preseason list along with the Katrina McClain Award preseason list. On Tuesday she was named to the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason list.

She is one of two Pac-12 players on the Hammon list.

In her first season playing for the Zags a year ago, Whittaker averaged 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game with 649 points and a school-record 348 rebounds.

Coach list

Lisa Fortier, who is entering her 13th season as head coach at Gonzaga, has been named to the Kathy Delaney-Smith Coach of the Year preseason watch list.

Fortier is one of 20 coaches nationally selected to the preseason list. The award is in its fourth season.

She enters the season four wins away from becoming the all-time winningest Gonzaga coach with a 313-84 overall record. That’s a .788 winning percentage. The winningest coach is Kelly Graves (316-136, .699), who is beginning his 13th season at Oregon.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women see plenty of bright spots in exhibition rout of Westmont
Gonzaga.summary:
As exhibitions go, it was true to form.

Dig deeper and it’s clear to see why there’s excitement about two teams that play in McCarthey Athletic Center.

Nearly a month to the day of its first preseason practice, the Gonzaga women’s basketball team showed it was ready to play Tuesday, cruising past the NCAA Division II Westmont College Warriors 84-43 before 4,490.

All 12 available Gonzaga players saw time in the first half, and a freshman made an emphatic debut.

Abby Lusk, the Zags’ lone freshman from Pocatello, Idaho, made the first two shots of her career, both 3-pointers, and had 10 points on 4 of 4 shooting in five minutes.

Impressive considering she had been out a week after spraining an ankle. Coach Lisa Fortier said Lusk was a game-time decision.

“It’s the little things that, like, Little Me dreamed about,” Lusk said of her debut. “Getting your first college baskets. It’s just a surreal moment. Being able to make two (back-to-back 3-pointers) is kind of fun too. Seeing the love and support from the bench and the girls on the court … it was everything I envisioned it being.”

Lusk finished with 12 points and four rebounds in 11 minutes.

“We wanted to get her under the lights and see how she did,” Fortier said. “And she did very well. … I think her parents would have come up if they would have known she was going to play. But we had no idea.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who was the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season, scored Gonzaga’s first basket. Whittaker ate up the smaller Warriors inside in the opening 20 minutes with 16 points on 6-of-8 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. She finished with a game-high 24 points, six rebounds and three assists in 21 minutes.

Four of five starters from a year ago started Tuesday and Mead High graduate and junior guard Teryn Gardner stepped into the lineup, replacing fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt.

The lone Zag not to play was sophomore forward Jaiden Haile, who was the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year last season. She was wearing a boot from an overuse injury. She started shooting in light practice last week.

Every Gonzaga player logged at least 10 minutes.

Another bright spot was the play of senior guard Zeryhia Aokuso. She scored from all areas, finishing with 14 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga asserted authority early in the third quarter, using a 7-0 spurt to set the tone. It was the most pleasing stretch for Fortier.

“The thing I liked the most was how we came out in the third,” Fortier said. “Hopefully our team is going to be a team that gets leads and then play from the front versus always coming from behind. We talked at halftime about what our energy was going to look like in the third. I thought it was really good energy, probably our best quarter.”

It was the second game in two days for Westmont, from Santa Barbara, California. The Warriors fell 71-46 at Washington State on Sunday.

Gonzaga opens the season with three straight home games, beginning Monday when North Dakota State visits. The Bison are picked to win the Summit League championship.

NDSU is similar to Gonzaga. The Bison return four of five starters including a Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year.

Gonzaga opened the season at NDSU last year, winning 81-66.

“North Dakota State is really good,” Fortier said. “So it’s a tough opener. Hopefully we’ll get the best work we can in the next few days.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women show off versatility, experience during Fan Fest scrimmage
Gonzaga.summary:
Most Fan Fest’s are a happy-go-lucky time, nothing more than an opportunity to put the jersey on for the first time and take to the court under the lights.

For the Gonzaga women’s basketball team, Saturday was different. The Zags didn’t just want to go through the motions. Ten of them played in the Fan Fest a year ago and they weren’t happy with the product they put on display.

Yes, the Zags were squaring off against their teammates, their friends. But judging by the competitiveness, it meant something to them.

Few will remember the score or which color prevailed come March. But for the record, Blue, led by Lauren Whittaker, Ines Bettencourt and Teryn Gardner, topped White 42-30 in the 20-minute scrimmage at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Equivalent to half a game, Whittaker, the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season had 12 points, five rebounds, two assists and two steals. Bettencourt, who is seeking a fifth year of eligibility and is presently eligible, had 10 points and Gardner, who is vying for a starting position and more playing time this season, had nine points on 3-of-6 shooting from 3-point range.

Gonzaga was the top 3-point shooting team in the nation, and the Zags will likely be among the leaders again this season. Blue and White combined to make 9 of 18 from distance.

But as the scrimmage showed, the Zags can do a number of things. And there’s much room for improvement. Coach Lisa Fortier, who along with dedicated assistants Stacy Clinesmith, Jordan Green and husband, Craig Fortier, begin their 13th season, will watch the Fan Fest video.

“We’ll go back and see all the problem areas,” Fortier said. “Half the time I was talking to my friends (during the scrimmage). So we’ll definitely go back and watch (the video).”

As she always does at Fan Fest, Fortier left the in-game coaching to her assistants.

“I liked how we were trying to push the ball (in transition), get the ball outletted faster, run the floor harder,” Fortier said. “We’ve done it in a little bit different way in the past where we’ve had the point guard really pass it full court. So last year we got bogged down a little bit with too many dribbles in transition. So I thought our team ran hard and looked to (pass) the ball to people. We didn’t always score in transition, but we’re getting those opportunities.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile sat out, her left foot still in a boot recovering from what she called an overuse injury. She said she expects to be back in two to three weeks.

Eleven of 12 Zags scored. Interestingly, the one who didn’t, junior guard Allie Turner, won the 3-point shooting contest. She edged Gardner. Turner and Gardner led the Zags in 3-point shooting last year.

All three new Zags - freshman Abby Lusk and transfers Emmy Roach and Jocelyn Medina - scored. Roach led with six points.

Bettencourt had an interesting passing partner during the 3-point shooting contest - former UConn teammate Azzi Fudd, the No. 1 draft pick by the Dallas Wings in the 2025 WNBA draft.

All five returning starters made cases for securing their starting job. And Gardner is certainly making a case to be a starter.

“There are people who are more likely (to start) based on their tenure here,” Fortier said. “Last year we ended up starting the same lineup (every game). That’s kind of been our style, but we’re always trying to not have that be a thing. You have to earn it every day in practice and even after you’ve gotten it that doesn’t mean you get it forever.”

Bettencourt thought the Zags did a number of things well Saturday.

“I mean, what is there not to like,” Bettencourt said. “We started off strong with our (drill) competitions - what we can do individually and then in the scrimmage. We were just having fun. It’s always better to be playing in front of a crowd instead of a silent gym and the coaches yelling at us constantly. It was just good to be back in front of the fans.”

That’s why they call it Fan Fest.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with experience, Gonzaga women appear better than ever ahead of annual Fan Fest
Gonzaga.summary:
When it comes to the Gonzaga women’s basketball team’s Fan Fest, it’s less about execution and more about embracing the moment.

More than anything, it’s the first opportunity for the Zags to wear their uniforms and step onto the court at McCarthey Athletic Center in a pseudo-competitive environment. Just because the Bulldogs aren’t playing a real opponent, playing against each other can bring out the competitive spirit.

After all, teammates don’t like to lose to teammates – whether it’s a table-top game, a 3-point shooting contest or an intrasquad scrimmage.

That alone is reason for a crowd to show up Saturday when things tip off at 2 p.m. and fans can get their first look at the 2026-27 lineup.

Junior point guard Allie Turner, who has started nearly all Gonzaga games since her arrival from St. Louis, Missouri, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

Turner hopes the Zags put forward a better showing than a year ago.

“Hopefully we’re way better than last year,” Turner said of Fan Fest. “I remember some people being like ‘(we) should have moved (Fan Fest) back a few weeks last year.’ But hopefully this year we look like a well-oiled machine out there.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier was told that Turner brought up Fan Fest and her expectation of making a better debut this year.

“It’s funny that Allie brought up Fan Fest. I don’t even remember it to be honest with you,” Fortier said.

Fortier won’t be looking at the final statistics. She doesn’t put much stock in who scores what or who has the most rebounds in a scrimmage.

“The big thing is getting them under the lights,” Fortier said. “It’s good to see where everyone is. For me it’s good for my coaches to get to coach. I sit on the side and rib everybody and take notes.”

Ten of the 13 Zags have suited up for a Fan Fest. It’ll be a new experience for freshman forward Abby Lusk, GU’s lone incoming frosh from Pocatello, Idaho; guard Emmy Roach, a junior transfer from Rider University; and guard Jocelyn Medina, a senior transfer from Denver.

A roster is usually needed for Fan Fest. Not this year. Even returning is graduate guard Ines Bettencourt, who gained a fifth year of eligibility this summer late under the new 5-in-5 eligibility format. So her former uniform number (8) had been assigned to Medina. Bettencourt’s new number is 0.

Former Mead standout Teryn Gardner, who transferred from Boise State last year and made an immediate impact coming off the bench, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

“We have basically the same team back so I think we’re all super excited for that,” Gardner said. “It’s going to be a fun time.”

Gardner said the goal for Fan Fest isn’t anything complicated.

“We want to start solidifying our plays,” she said. “We want to help the three new girls get to know everything and how we run the system and whatnot. We want to have fun but we want to make it a good scrimmage.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile will be sitting on the sideline. She’s still wearing a boot on a foot she injured during the summer. The injury is healing and doesn’t appear to be longterm, Fortier said.

Haile was selected as the West Coast Conference Sixth Woman of the Year last season.

Fortier has been cautious with Haile’s recovery.

A deep roster

It stands to figure Gonzaga will be a much more polished team this year.

But there are questions to be answered. Can GU win a championship in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12? Can it win an NCAA Tournament game and go further than any previous GU team? With all five starters back, does coach Fortier just roll out the 2025-26 starting lineup? And with five other returners who got quality playing time, how does Fortier divvy up minutes?

Lots of questions and no hurry to come up with answers.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Fortier has decided to stay away from concrete specified goals with her team this year.

“We’re not even really setting those in the same way,” Fortier said. “Our team goal is to show up every day in practice. We’re not even putting that (goals) to paper. We talk about the process a lot. I think it does them a disservice to (talk about goals). They may or may not have those in the back of their heads, but we’re not gonna verbalize those things. I believe if we show up every day and try to get better then all of the end is going to take care of itself.”

Fortier is right. There will be much conversation about potential by a number of people – right, wrong or indifferent – so the Zags would do themselves favors by veering away from those conversations.

They know, for example, they’ll have a target on their backs. With essentially the whole team back they can’t help but be picked to win the Pac-12 Conference and advance to the NCAA Tournament.

There will also be talk of the potential to be the best team ever under Fortier and best in school history. But it does the Zags no good to get caught up in those expectations.

Gonzaga is going to be good. The Zags know it. The Bulldogs will be out to stack days together. And that could get them to where they want to go.

Gonzaga.title: Experienced Gonzaga women return Ines Bettencourt after court ruling: 'It's a new energy'
Gonzaga.summary:
Expectations are going to be high for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team in 2026-27.

A late addition to the roster now may blow those expectations through the roof of McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags were set to essentially return their entire team from 2025-26 with the exception of guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring.

The NCAA’s new five-years-to-play-five-seasons eligibility model announced this summer opened the door for the Portugal native to fight for an additional year of eligibility. She joined a California class action lawsuit, gaining a temporary restraining order and immediate eligibility.

Bettencourt returned to Spokane on Sept. 5.

Now the band is back together for Gonzaga, which will have one of the deepest rosters in the nation with 10 returners, including five starters to go with two transfers and one freshman.

Bettencourt and GU coach Lisa Fortier were cautious in calling it a done deal when the Zags took the court for their first preseason practice last week. A preliminary hearing on Tuesday in Santa Clara County appeared to push a final decision to October 20, at the earliest. 

The Zags are proceeding as if they’ll have Bettencourt.

“It’s been a long summer ever since I graduated,” said Bettencourt, who went back to Portugal and practiced frequently with her national team. “I kind of knew that this would be a possibility. So I was just working behind the scenes and talking with Lisa (Fortier), not really telling anyone else because it wasn’t for sure.”

As soon as the NCAA adopted the new eligibility format, Bettencourt began talking to Fortier and Gonzaga compliance officials “to figure out what exactly I have to do to come back because as an international it’s harder to come back than an American.”

There Bettencourt was going through drills and running up and down the court with her teammates like she had never left.

“Like McKynnlie (Dalan, senior forward) said, ‘we set you off, (had) all these goodbyes and now you’re back.’ ”

Fortier said Gonzaga will proceed as if Bettencourt will be eligible the whole season.

“She had asked us pretty early on in April or May (about coming back) and she was kind of joking at first,” Fortier said. “No one actually thought that any of this was gonna happen. The answer was like sure (you can come back).”

Bettencourt is stoked to have another year with her coaches and what she calls her “best friends.”

“Just having one more shot at this, making the (NCAA) Tournament. Just being more prepared for whatever’s next for me,” Bettencourt said. “So it’s just awesome. Everyone was happy for me.”

Fortier is overjoyed to have Bettencourt back – something the Zags never thought would be an option four months ago.

“She’s one of ours so we would love to have her back,” Fortier said. “She shows up every day around the program and she takes care of business like a professional. She’s a pro in all ways.”

The familiarity will be a team strength no doubt.

“We know each other,” Bettencourt said. “So it was just super nice for them to receive me well again.”

Bettencourt spent most of the summer playing 3-on-3 in Portugal. It was different preparation for returning to Gonzaga.

“I have to run more now,” Bettencourt said, smiling.

Bettencourt took over a leadership role last year as the team’s lone senior. Now as a graduate, she wants to continue to lean into leadership.

“Just building on the leadership,” she said.

She expects to be a better player, too.

“Stay composed and stay consistent at everything,” she said about her personal expectations. “I’m just taking it day by day because I get to come back and be with my teammates, with my coaches, and practice with them again.”

Junior point guard Allie Turner started alongside Bettencourt in the backcourt last year. Turner, Bettencourt and sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker all lived together last year.

The trio can’t run that arrangement back as living assignments had already been passed out. But Turner is glad to have Bettencourt along for one more year.

“We’re super happy to have her back,” Turner said. “It’s a new energy.”

Whittaker agreed.

“For a long time we didn’t really think it was an option. And then kind of a quick turnaround within a couple of weeks we heard (she) was coming back,” Whittaker said. “She’s a player that I think is really seamless to bring back to the team. She has a lot of experience and was a great leader last year and obviously a great player. So it was kind of just an easy transition for her and everyone has been really supportive of it. It’s kind of like she’s never left.”

Bettencourt is looking forward to returning to McCarthey Athletic Center and seeing the fans for FanFest on Oct. 10.

“Super excited,” Bettencourt said. “I’m sure they (the fans) are going to be like ‘what? What are you doing here again?’ But I’m super excited to be back in front of all the fans with my team and showing them again what we can bring this year.”

Oregon State.title: No Reason To Panic About Oregon State Football's Pac-12 Hopes
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State suffered a tough loss this past weekend against the Fresno State Bulldogs, a performance that gives this Beavers' squad some real adversity to deal with after five consecutive wins. That being said, there's still plenty left for the Beavers to accomplish this season despite now having three losses on their record.

Your host Matt Bagley gives his reaction to what went right and what went wrong for Oregon State in that game, and why there should be no reason to panic despite the mistakes of JaMarcus Shephard's team.

It's also time to look ahead to a matchup against a tricky Texas State team, who pushed Boise State to their limits. It could be a return to form for #Pac12AfterDark. Hear JaMarcus Shephard's Monday comments in the buildup to that matchup.

Meanwhile on the hardwood, Justin Joyner's men's basketball had a strong opening win against Weber State. It was an encouraging, well-rounded display with all of the Beavers' toughest obstacles still yet to come.  

All that, and the five college football games that you should watch this Saturday. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Effects of Jesse Legree's Commitment To OSU + 2026 Basketball Previews
Oregon State.summary:
One of the biggest stories in college football of the last two weeks: Oregon State freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree making a formal commitment to the Beavers through the 2027-2028 season.  For a good chunk of this week's episode of State of the Beavs, we're looking at that decision and what it means for the overall growth of the program - even if JaMarcus Shephard would rather take things one game at a time. 

You'll hear clips both from Shephard's media availability coming out of the bye week, and from Legree's announcement at his high school in Baltimore before we look at the Beavers' matchup with Fresno State in California on Halloween. 

With just a few days before the start of college basketball season, it's also time to look at the Beaver men's and women's programs. John Severs and Ben Pahl were present at Oregon State's media day in Portland last week and join the show to offer their perspectives.

All that, plus the five college football games that you need to watch over Halloween weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Questions Following Oregon State Football's 5-2 Start To 2026
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State are one win away from reaching bowl eligibility in JaMarcus Shephard's first season as head coach after a 48-30 victory against the Washington State Cougars. Of course, we dive into a recap of the action from that contest as Jesse Legree, AJ Newberry, and the rest of the Beavers continue to spearhead a monumental turnaround. Hear audio from Takari Hickle and Trey Glasper about that result.

However, it's also important to note that after the contest, Shephard was quick to offer condolences to the families of the victims of last weeks' tragic shooting in Bend at Silver Rail Elementary.  Hear Shephard's comments, and why they matter to the state and the college football community at-large.

After that, your host Matt Bagley dives into three questions that have arisen in our minds about the Beavers' season following the hot start.

All that, and the five college football games you should watch this week as the Beavers get a bye week to prepare for a road matchup with Fresno State to close the month of October. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Jesse Legree Continues To Set Records For Oregon State Football
Oregon State.summary:
En route to a 4-2 record for Oregon State football, true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree has been one of the most electrifying players in the country.  The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Looks To Sustain Momentum Against San Diego State
Oregon State.summary:
To start their first conference schedule in the relaunched Pac-12, the Oregon State Beavers picked up a blowout win over Colorado State this past weekend. Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree continued their impressive run of form and the tight ends also got heavily involved en route to the 56-26 result. Time to review that result and what else worked for JaMarcus Shephard to get his team to a 3-2 record on the year.

This Saturday, the Beavers host a 2-3 San Diego State squad, who are coming off of a dramatic 31-29 win over the Texas State Bobcats. What challenges does Sean Lewis' team present to the Beavers as the Aztecs deal with a mumps outbreak? In addition to our thoughts, you'll hear clips from Shephard's media availability, as well as offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen and defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre.

All that, plus a look at the five college football games that Matt Bagley thinks you should watch this weekend. 

Thank you for your support of the show, and as always, Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Returns to a Pac-12 Schedule
Oregon State.summary:
After a win over the UTEP Miners in El Paso, the Oregon State Beavers are 2-2 under the direction of JaMarcus Shephard. While many Power Conference programs around the nation likely wouldn't be satisfied with that type of start, it's important to keep perspective on the progress made in Shephard's first several months leading the team. 

As your host Matt Bagley looks at that, you'll also hear audio from JaMarcus Shephard's Monday press conference. Oregon State travels to Fort Collins this week for their Pac-12 opener against the Colorado State Rams. 

In between all the football talk, we also take some time to discuss the No. 21 Oregon State men's soccer team with our own John Severs, as they get into the home stretch of the 2026 season.

All that, and a look at the five games that you should watch during your college football weekend. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: The College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams. What does it mean for WSU?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The college football ecosystem changed in a seismic way Monday.

The College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams beginning next season, opening up more spots for more teams, but also opening doors to untold amounts of other consequences.

What does it all mean for Washington State? It’s a tricky question, but here are the top ramifications of the CFP’s expansion, which carves out only one guaranteed spot for the highest-ranked Group of 6 team.

Next season, WSU’s nonconference schedule includes a home game against rival Washington (the second-to-last Apple Cup currently under contract), a home matchup against Kansas and a road game against Arizona. Under the new rules set by the CFP’s expansion, one of which requires Power 4 teams to play 10 Power 4 games each season, those games might be in jeopardy for WSU, which is now regarded as a Group of 6 program – but there’s a catch for the Cougars.

For 2027, legacy Pac-12 members WSU and Oregon State will be treated as Power 4 programs, according to a report from CBS Sports. That means the Cougars’ Power 4 games for next season are expected to be safe, and they won’t have to do any short-notice rescheduling.

What is unclear is how WSU and OSU will be treated in 2028 and beyond. If they aren’t regarded as P4 programs, several of the Cougs’ future games could be in jeopardy, including a 2028 road game against Kansas, a 2029 home game against Kansas State, a 2031 home game against Virginia and a 2032 road game against Texas Tech.

Here are the current nonconference schedules of WSU’s Power 4 opponents in 2028 and beyond, which will need to be tweaked.

2028 Washington: vs. WSU, vs. Eastern Washington, vs. UNLV

2028 Kansas: at Hawaii, vs. Lindenwood (FCS), vs. WSU

2029 Kansas State: at WSU, vs. Sam Houston

2031 Virginia: at WSU, vs. Richmond (FCS)

2032 Texas Tech: vs. WSU, vs. Fresno State, at UTEP

If those games don’t come to fruition for the Cougars and if Power 4 teams don’t schedule nonconference games against Group of 6 opponents, their opportunities to bolster their resume become few and far between. G6 teams have a hard enough time making the playoff, appearing only four times since it began in 2014. Can they convince the playoff committee they deserve another spot if their only opponents are other G6 teams and FCS foes?

The CFP’s expansion also casts more doubt on the future of the Apple Cup, which is set to be played in 2027 in Pullman and 2028 in Seattle, but no games are under contract beyond that. In recent days, the Huskies and Cougars have expressed interest in continuing the 118-year series – WSU President Betsy Cantwell indicated as much at a CougsFirst! event in Spokane over the weekend, while UW AD Pat Chun said there is “an intent to try and continue the game on both sides” in a radio interview – but the potential incentive for the series’ continuation is another factor.

The Power 4 Huskies will be required to play 10 P4 games, which means one P4 nonconference game. Would UW, which has placed a high priority on hosting seven home games per year, be interested in scheduling WSU as one of its two remaining games? Power-conference schools usually schedule one FCS game each season, which go a long way in funding FCS programs’ athletic departments. That leaves one open spot, and it’s unclear whether UW would want to schedule WSU to fill it.

Think about it this way from the Huskies’ perspective: If they beat the Cougars, they’ll have done what they’re expected to, which wouldn’t do much to move the needle for their playoff chances. If they lose to the Cougs, their resume would include a loss to a G6 team, which could mean a big hit to their chances. The Apple Cup clearly means a lot to the state of Washington, but it’s also true that UW has a lot more to lose than to gain from the series continuing.

From WSU’s side: A win over UW would do wonders for the Cougars’ resume. A loss wouldn’t do much at all.

The CFP’s expansion to 24 teams creates more wiggle room for losses – if the 24-team field existed this year, the CFP announced, it would include teams like 4-5 Iowa State and 3-6 Colorado – so it’s possible neither WSU nor UW would take a big hit from a loss in the Apple Cup.

Another tenet of the CFP’s expansion: The Power 4 leagues have each announced they are ending their conference championship games, a major change to preserve their teams’ chances of making the playoff field. But the Pac-12 has not announced it will follow suit, nor have other G6 conferences, which will have to weigh two factors. Do they keep the conference championship games, which figure to be lucrative broadcast events and help make their champions more clear-cut candidates for the field? Or do they cancel them, which could protect the highest-ranked team but remove a revenue stream?

“I saw the headline. I saw the headline maybe about conference championships getting nixed as well,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said Monday in his weekly news conference. “I don’t think it necessarily changes our path, right? So whether it’s 12, whether it’s 24, our path’s our path, and we gotta focus on that.”

Group of 6 programs like WSU have a better chance of making the playoff, which is opening up 12 more spots. But in the CFP’s 12-year history, only four G5/G6 teams have made the field: Cincinnati in 2021, Boise State in 2025 (the first year of the 12-team format), plus Tulane and James Madison in 2026. Each has lost its first game in the playoff.

Could the Cougars make the playoff one day? It’s possible. But it’s also possible that teams of their ilk face a steeper climb into the 24-team field than the 12-team iteration.

Washington State.title: Boise State and Texas State on top as Broncos churn toward a CFP berth | Pac-12 power rankings for Week 11
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

The dynamics of the inaugural Pac-12 season have changed dramatically in the past few weeks.

At the mid-October turn, for example, Oregon State looked unbeatable and Utah State looked entirely beatable.

Now? The Beavers have lost back-to-back games, and the Aggies have won two in a row.

A few weeks ago, Texas State was under .500 and facing a steep climb to bowl-eligibility.

Now? The Bobcats have won three of their past four, walloped Oregon State and are churning toward an appearance in the conference championship game.

One component has remained fixed: Boise State was the team to beat last month and is the team to beat this month, with a two-game lead in the conference race and only three weeks remaining.

And based on the initial College Football Playoff rankings, the Broncos (8-1) are the frontrunner to claim the bid reserved for the top team in the Group of Six.

In that regard, their competitive position strengthened exponentially over the weekend thanks to three results:

• The Broncos steamed to victory at Colorado State.

• Oregon won at Ohio State, thereby adding credibility to Boise State’s narrow early-season loss in Eugene.

• And UT-San Antonio, the top team in the American, was beaten soundly by Florida Atlantic, sideswiping what appeared to be Boise State’s chief competitor for the CFP berth.

At this point, the Broncos have a decisive advantage over all other Group of Six teams in ESPN’s strength-of-record rankings, which closely approximate one of the most important metrics used by the CFP selection committee.

Here are the top Group of Six teams in strength of record, which measures how a team performs against its schedule compared to how an average team would fare against the same lineup of opponents.

(With national ranking.)

No. 20: Boise State

No. 30: New Mexico

No. 35: Louisiana Tech

No. 39: North Texas

No. 40: Liberty

No. 42: UTSA

Positions can shift markedly based on a single result. Prior to losing to Florida Atlantic, for instance, UTSA was within a few spots of Boise State.

But it has become increasingly clear that the Broncos control their fate — that by winning out, they will lock up the coveted CFP berth for the second time in three years.

If they lose once? Well, the situation could get dicey.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (8-1/5-0)

Result: won at Colorado State 64-38

Next up: vs. Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: ESPN’s popular ‘College GameDay’ show is heading to Boise this week despite Oregon State’s two-game losing streak. It will be the third ‘GameDay’ appearance in the Mountain Time Zone in the past five weeks, following October stops in Provo and Salt Lake City. (Last week: 1)

2. Texas State (5-4/3-2)

Result: won at Oregon State 42-21

Next up: vs. Fresno State (1 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: Getting easier (by the minute) to both envision the Bobcats facing Boise State for the Pac-12 championship — it would be a rematch of their Halloween thriller — and to wonder what might have been if Texas State hadn’t lost to UTSA and San Diego State by a combined seven points. (Last week: 5)

3. Fresno State (5-4/2-3)

Result: lost at Utah State 17-10

Next up: at Texas State (1 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The Hotline assumed the Bulldogs, fresh off the win over Oregon State, would have a stopover in Letdown City on their way to Logan. Admittedly, we didn’t count on them getting stuck there overnight. (Last week: 2)

4. Oregon State (5-4/3-2)

Result: lost to Texas State 42-21

Next up: at Boise State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: That would be 80 points and 992 yards allowed by the Beavers in the past two games. But the bigger issue is the complete collapse of their previously unstoppable offense. (Last week: 3)

5. Utah State (4-5/3-2)

Result: beat Fresno State 17-10

Next up: at San Diego State (6:30 p.m. USA Network)

Comment: Coach Bronco Mendenhall is too good for his team to wallow for an entire season. We’re kicking ourselves for thinking otherwise, even for just a few weeks. (Last week: 6)

6. San Diego State (4-5/3-2)

Next up: vs. Utah State (6:30 p.m. USA Network)

Comment: There are two examples, Utah State and Texas State, of teams playing better in November than they did in October. Will the Aztecs be the third? Or will they meander to the finish? (Last week: 4)

Next up: at Washington State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: The Rams have the worst total defense and scoring defense in the country, and it’s not even close. How this happened under Jim Mora is one of the most fascinating subplots of the inaugural Pac-12 season. (Last week: 7)

Washington State.title: Favored by more than a touchdown, WSU set to host Colorado State | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against Colorado State on Saturday night.

What is it?

Fresh off its only bye week of the year, WSU is set to host Colorado State to kick off the final stretch of the season. The Cougars are on a six-game losing streak and heading into Week 11, they’re still looking for their first FBS win of the season. They’re mired in their worst season since 2009, when they finished 1-11.

While the teams have met several times in the last few years, this will be the first meeting between WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) and CSU (3-6, 1-4) in Pullman since 2022.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 7:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

CBS Sports Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

WSU opened as a 91/2-point favorite

How did the Cougars fare last week?

WSU was off last week, enjoying its one and only bye week of the season, a policy in both the rebuilt and traditional Pac-12. The Cougars had the latest bye week in the conference, alongside San Diego State.

The week before, WSU fell in a 26-20 road loss to San Diego State, making the Cougars 0-5 on the road this fall. Coach Kirby Moore’s team made things interesting in the fourth quarter, drawing within one score on a rushing touchdown by quarterback Owen Eshelman, but the visitors’ comeback fizzled out with a turnover on downs later in the fourth frame.

Eshelman and the Cougs’ offense looked OK, but that group again got next to nothing from its rushing attack, which netted only 68 yards and one touchdown – 34 yards from running backs. In nine FBS games, those three tailbacks – Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi – are averaging only 46 yards on 15 carries.

On the other side of the ball, WSU’s defense forced one turnover, an interception from safety Jaylen Thomas on a pass tipped by linebacker Keith Brown. But that was only the Cougars’ sixth forced turnover of the season, which is two spots up from dead last in the country. And for the second straight game, they also did not pick up any sacks, leaving them with just eight on the season – No. 134 of 138 FBS teams.

WSU’s perimeter tackling also led to several big SDSU plays, including two rushing touchdowns from tailback Javion Kinnard, who made WSU defensive backs Jamarey Smith and Khamari Terrell miss on his two scoring plays. In all, the Cougars whiffed on 10 tackles, according to Pro Football Focus. They’ve missed double-digit tackles in six of their eight FBS games.

Scouting Colorado State…

Under first-year head coach Jim Mora and quarterback Hauss Hejny, Colorado State has lost six of its last seven games, in large part due to its defense. The Rams rank last in the country in scoring defense by a wide margin, giving up an average of 44 points per game, and their 542 yards given up per game is also last in the country.

Earlier this year, Mora relieved defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of his playcalling duties midgame. Summers left the field and subsequently the program.

That move has not helped Colorado State’s cause, however. The Rams’ last win was a 56-49 victory over San Diego State in late October, but since then, they’ve dropped games to Utah State and Boise State.

The Rams are coming off a 64-38 loss to first-place Boise State, permitting a total of 669 yards to the Broncos’ offense led by backup quarterback Max Cutforth. In that game, CSU offensive lineman Toriyan Johnson and strength coach Shelton Bynum were seen arguing on the sideline. On the field, the Rams yielded 352 yards rushing and 317 yards passing.

“I’ve been doing this a long time, and I’ve never been involved with something like this,” Mora said after that game. “So it’s disappointing.”

On the season, Colorado State has given up the following point totals: 13, 24, 41, 59, 56, 66, 49, 31, 64. The Rams are also allowing an average of 8.4 yards per play, which is last in the country, as is their percentage of defensive drives that result in touchdowns: 52%.

But even Colorado State’s 10 sacks rank better than WSU’s eight. And the Rams rank first in the conference in both forced fumbles (eight) and interceptions (nine).

On offense, CSU is led by Hejny, who has completed 104 of 159 passes (65%) for 1,391 yards and 16 touchdowns against two interceptions, ranking third in the Pac-12 with 231 passing yards a pop. The Rams’ top tailback is Auburn transfer Durell Robinson, who has registered 104 carries for 449 yards and nine touchdowns, including a 117-yard game against Oregon State and a 66-yard outing against Boise State last weekend. Their top receiver is former Division II transfer RJ Vick, who has posted 32 catches for 463 yards and four touchdowns.

Fellow CSU running back Mel Brown, who transferred from UConn along with Mora, has been limited lately. He played only six snaps against Boise State, and before missing the previous game against Utah State, he logged just 10 snaps against San Diego State.

What happened last time?

WSU and CSU’s last clash came last season in Fort Collins, where the Cougars ground out a 20-3 win, their defense handing the Rams one of their two touchdown-less games that season.

Washington State.title: WSU GETS HOT FROM THREE, BUT FALL AS HIGH POINT DEFENDS HOME COURT
WSU MBB: David Riley | High Point Postgame | 11/7/26
Cougars Fall in Tight Battle at Oregon, 64-57
WSU WBB: Kamie Ethridge | Oregon Postgame | 11/6/26
WSU unwinds in second half in 83-71 loss to High Point, opening season with two straight setbacks
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Since David Riley took over as Washington State’s head coach, his teams have faced all kinds of problems, from defense to turnovers to an unsightly combination of the two.

When things get tight in the second half, and their opponent hits them with a surge of six or seven straight points, Riley’s teams have also struggled to respond. Those sequences have almost always spelled doom for the Cougs.

That was the story of WSU’s 83-71 road loss to High Point on Saturday afternoon, the Cougars’ second straight loss to open the season. It’s also the second straight season WSU has started with two straight setbacks.

“Our interior defense. That was the biggest thing,” said WSU coach David Riley, whose team allowed High Point to shoot 58% from the field. “We didn’t guard the ball, and when we did, we fouled. You’re not gonna win on the road against an NCAA Tournament team when you give up that many free throws, when you let them shoot 68% from the field in the second half. Our defense just wasn’t good enough.”

Transfer guard Lazerek Houston poured in a game-best 31 points and wing Jaylen Harrell posted 18 for the Cougars, who took a 52-50 lead midway through the second half on a long triple from guard RJ Jones, who totaled 12 points. But on the next possession, Jones was whistled for a technical foul, slowing the flow of the game and taking away momentum from WSU.

High Point followed with a 10-2 run, seizing control of the game, and Washington State didn’t have the horses to respond. The Cougars, who converted 12 of 26 shots from beyond the arc, kept things within five and six points for the next several minutes. But when the Panthers widened their lead to double digits, the visitors couldn’t bring it back.

“We gotta learn how to handle success better,” Riley said. “We hit a couple shots, we’re flowing, and all of a sudden, after that, they started getting to the rim at will. We can’t get distracted, and in a game like this, we gotta have more leadership than that. That can’t happen.”

Riley’s teams have not been known for their defense. In the Cougars’ season-opening loss to Davidson at the beginning of the week, they allowed the Wildcats to shoot 55% from the field, including 63% in the second half. On Saturday, they surrendered a similar performance to the Panthers, who followed the Jones technical with a long triple and back-to-back dunks.

Part of the problem at play for WSU was the presence of Houston, who is listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds. He can really fill it up on offense, and he might be the best shot-creator on the team. But because of his lack of size, he makes for an easy target on defense, and High Point took advantage, going right at him. That included a nice game from guard CJ Brown, who tallied 17 points.

The Cougars played a second straight game without key wing transfer Ronnie Harrison, who turned his ankle hours before Monday’s game against Davidson, Riley said. It’s unclear when Harrison might be able to return. Without him, the Cougs are missing one of their best players, a two-way force whose defense could stabilize this group.

Either way, it goes down as a loss for WSU, which returns to action on Tuesday at Duquesne. The Cougars played a solid game in the first half, opening the contest on a 7-0 run and keeping their lead for most of the second half. Houston looked electric all night, knocking down 5 of 8 shots from deep and 9 of 13 overall. It’s clear he will play a key role for this WSU team.

But Houston and Harrell didn’t get much help. Jones hit four triples for 12 points, but outside of that, here are the WSU scorers: Ladji Dembele and Sebastian Akins had three points apiece, while Casey Jones and Fraser Roxburgh posted two points each. Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, who has started each of his team’s two games, has gone scoreless in each.

But in these two second halves, the Cougars have been undone by their defense. They’ll get a chance to turn that around on Tuesday on the road against Duquesne, which moved to 2-0 after holding on for a close win against Division-II Central State (Ohio) on Saturday.

“This is a team that can guard,” Riley said, “and it really is frustrating to see us give up easy shots at the rim. That’s way too high a percentage, and we gotta do better than that.”

Washington State.title: Gardner Minshew reminds reporters how Mike Leach rerouted him from Alabama to WSU
Washington State.summary:
Veteran NFL quarterback Gardner Minshew was recently named the starting quarterback for the Arizona Cardinals.

In a recent press conference, Minshew reminded reporters that he was going to play college football at Alabama, but late coaching legend Mike Leach changed his mind.

“I was going to Alabama to be a third-string and then to be a GA (Graduate Assistant) and coach,” Minshew said. “And I was fired up to do that, it was awesome.”

Before committing to Alabama, Minshew had a conversation with Leach, who was Washington State’s head coach at the time.

“Coach Leach asked do I want to go hold a clipboard or lead the country in passing?,” Minshew recalled.

Leach’s pitch worked to get Minshew to Washington State in 2018, where he threw for the second-most yards in the NCAA.

Minshew ended up throwing for 38 touchdowns and 4,779 yards in one season with Leach, which helped him get selected in the sixth round of the NFL Draft.

Minshew has played in the NFL for eight years, and the veteran quarterback credited a lot of his success to Leach.

“I can’t overstate what going to Washington State and playing for Coach Leach did for me,” Minshew said.

Washington State.title: WSU opens season with 76-61 loss to Davidson, dropping season-opener for second straight year
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – These days, college basketball seasons always arrive with an alluring sense of promise. The slate is clean, the roster is new, and the coach talks about how much he learned from last year and how different things will be in this one.

At Washington State, these last two years have started like that. Coach David Riley has talked with optimism about what he learned from his first season, then his second. He’s felt better about each roster he’s had, he says. Each October, he’s vowed to play better defense and scale back the turnovers.

But the Cougars have not delivered on that kind of potential. Last fall, they opened their season with a home loss to Idaho. And here on Monday night, they began Riley’s third season with a home setback to Davidson, walking off the floor as the buzzer rang on a 76-61 defeat.

“This has been the case ever since I’ve been a coach,” Riley said. “You work on things throughout the fall, throughout the summer, you build an identity, then you go to that first exhibition game, the first scrimmage or whatever, and that goes out the window. These guys kind of forget, they lose their mind. You kind of shore it up. You get to the real games. Same thing happens. And I thought this is a great example of that.”

This was about as inauspicious as it gets for the Cougars, who shot just 35% from the floor, including 5 for 24 from beyond the arc. Trailing by as many as 19, WSU allowed Davidson to convert 55% of field goals, including 63% in the second half. Offense was a mud slog for the Cougars. It was like a hot knife through butter for the Wildcats, who sank 12 of their 23 tries from distance, six from returning starting guard Sam Brown.

Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell scored a team-best 13 points for WSU, which used a 10-0 run to make things interesting in the second half, drawing within 47-38. But the Wildcats followed by getting three straight layups, stretching their lead back out to double digits, where it stayed for the remainder of the game.

On offense, the Cougs got lots of good looks. They just couldn’t knock them down. After the game, Riley said this is “one of the best shooting teams I’ve coached,” but it didn’t show: Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips connected on just 2 of 9 shots from deep, Harrell and Wake Forest transfer Sebastian Akins went 1-for-3 and UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele misfired on all three he tried. TCU transfer guard RJ Jones also went 0-for-2.

What’s behind those misses? Riley diagnosed the problem by pointing to the way his group couldn’t flow from its first look to an alternative one – the second action, he likes to call them. That was a problem last year’s team dealt with. One game into this season, these Cougars appear to have the same issue.

“It’s like right now in the offense, we freeze up after that first action, and all of a sudden we don’t know where those shots are coming from,” Riley said. “It’s hard to have confidence in those shots. You kinda get a random look, and you’re not ready for it, and I think some of that is just confidence. It’s hard to win when one team shoots 52% from three, and we shot 20.”

WSU played this game without East Texas A&M transfer Ronnie Harrison, who turned his ankle during pregame shootaround, Riley said. Harrison logged a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds in the Cougars’ exhibition win over Washington last week, and with his do-it-all skillset, he figures to play a central role on this team. Listed at 6-foot-8 and 228 pounds, Harrison is a senior and a compelling athlete, making his absence a big one for his group.

Riley hopes Harrison can play in WSU’s next game, a road test against High Point on Saturday, but he isn’t sure because the injury happened so soon before Monday’s game. If he’s out again, it’s a serious development for the Cougs, who need his shot-creation abilities and his veteran presence. It’s hard to overstate how big a loss Harrison’s is.

But on Monday, would he have turned a loss into a win? It’s hard to say. The Cougars looked disjointed on both sides of the ball. They gave up too many open triples to the Wildcats, who made offense look easy. Then they missed too many of those looks on offense. WSU has 14 newcomers, which Riley talked about after the game, and it’s not easy jelling that many players into a read-and-react system like Riley’s.

“It was clear we were on our heels a little bit all game,” Riley said. “It looked like a team with a bunch of newcomers playing a team with three returning starters that kinda knew what’s what.”

After the game, Harrell attributed part of this loss to effort, saying, “I feel like our effort wasn’t the way it was…. We practice hard every day. Since the summertime, we’ve been going at each other. We know what it takes to win, and I feel like today we didn’t show what we really had. That wasn’t the team that I play with all year. So we’re gonna get it right.”

That’s certainly not where the Cougars want to be after Game 1, talking about effort. Riley was relayed Harrell’s comments. Did he agree?

“It’s hard to think and play at the same time,” Riley said, “and I think that these guys want to go out there and compete. But when they’re thinking and they’re timid out there because they’re thinking, it looks the way it did.”

WSU has lots of time to turn this around, to make a second-straight season-opening home loss look like an exception to the rule. But it’s not a particularly encouraging start to the season for the Cougars, who now get a road game against a High Point team that won 31 games and made the NCAA Tournament second round last year.
