Washington State.title: 5 thoughts from WSU's loss to San Diego State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO – At some point in the fourth quarter, not long after Washington State angled toward mounting a comeback against San Diego State in Saturday’s game, things began to feel a bit eerie.

Driving down the field, the Cougars were facing a 26-14 deficit. Moments later, quarterback Owen Eshelman pulled a read option and jogged untouched into the end zone, letting out a good scream as he did so. All of a sudden, as listless as this WSU effort felt only a few moments prior, the visitors were angling toward a comeback.

It conjured memories of a certain game from two years ago: In 2024, in a road game against San Diego State, the Cougars were looking at a 26-14 hole in the fourth quarter. They made up the ground in the fourth quarter, sandwiching two John Mateer touchdowns around a Buddah Al-Uqdah interception, a string of winning plays to pull off a stunning rally.

These Cougars had no such luck Saturday night. Their final drive petered out around midfield, where right tackle Jaylin Caldwell was called for a false start, coach Kirby Moore took his final timeout to prevent the ensuing 10-second runoff and Eshelman’s final two passes fell incomplete, handing the ball back to the Aztecs.

With six straight loss es, WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) has three games left to find its first FBS win of the season. The Cougars are idle next week, giving them a chance to rest for the first time after nine games.

Here are five thoughts from the game.

1. WSU has to generate more sacks

After nine games, the Cougars have generated only eight sacks, which ranks No. 134 of 138 FBS teams. That’s not exactly what Moore had in mind when he landed transfers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk out of the transfer portal last winter. WSU did not produce any sacks in Saturday’s game, the second straight sack-less game the team has played.

This season, McLain and Zunk have had few issues creating havoc in backfields, but the sacks have eluded them. On Saturday, they largely struck out on both fronts. WSU engineered only six pressures on SDSU redshirt freshman quarterback Stone Saunders, according to Pro Football Focus, including two from McLain and one from Zunk.

Simply put: The Cougars have to get more pressure on quarterbacks, and they have to bring them down when they have the chance. On one play in Saturday’s game, cornerback Khamari Terrell had Saunders wrapped up for what looked like an easy sack, but Saunders wiggled free.

2. It’s probably time to abandon the run game altogether

WSU running backs Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for only 34 yards on 14 carries, an average rush of 2.4 yards. Here is how they have fared in eight FBS games this season.

• Washington: 16 carries, 38 yards.

• Kansas State: 17 carries, 72 yards.

• Arizona: 17 carries, 59 yards.

• Fresno State: 12 carries, 45 yards.

• Utah State: 19 carries, 77 yards.

• Oregon State: 13 carries, 26 yards.

• Boise State: 10 carries, 20 yards.

• SDSU: 14 carries, 34 yards.

That comes out to an average of 15 carries for 46 yards, some of the worst numbers in the country. It’s clear the problem comes in large part from the Cougars’ offensive line, which can’t move bodies in short-yardage situations. Maybe that group can solve some things for its final three games of the season, but it’s more likely that WSU can find success by doing away with the running game for the most part.

3. Cougars’ perimeter tackling left a lot to be desired

WSU’s last two opponents, Boise State and San Diego State, were wise to realize something: They couldn’t generate many yards up the middle, where Cougar defensive linemen have done well to bottle things up, but they could very easily bounce to the outside and jet upfield.

That’s how SDSU running back Javion Kinnard scored both of his touchdowns, making WSU defenders like nickelback Jamarey Smith and Jeremiah Bernard miss on his way to the end zone. The Cougars missed 10 tackles in this one, according to PFF, which is better than the 16 they missed against Boise State.

But when you aren’t getting sacks and aren’t generating many turnovers – even with safety Jaylen Thomas’ interception, his third of the year, the Cougs have forced only six turnovers, which is tied for No. 121 nationally – you have to tackle well. WSU has not done so recently.

4. WSU’s offense sustained drives well, but finishing remains elusive

The Cougs converted 9 of 14 third downs in Saturday’s game, an encouraging development to one of the team’s biggest weaknesses all year, which allowed them to sustain several drives. They scored one touchdown on a drive that chewed up nearly five minutes and covered 75 yards, then another on a series that elapsed 6 minutes , 15 seconds and went 64 yards. WSU converted 5 of its first 6 third downs, including two on Eshelman keepers.

But the Cougs couldn’t always finish their long drives. In the third frame, they used up 6:25 to march 40 yards in 13 plays, but on a third-and-10, Eshelman showed his inexperience by committing a costly intentional grounding penalty, resulting in a loss of 14 yards.

That set up a fourth-and-long from the 35, which meant a 53-yard field goal try for kicker Jack Stevens. His attempt went wide left and well short, scuttled by the rainy and windy conditions.

The Cougs also missed a chance to capitalize on Thomas’ interception, which landed their offense at the Aztecs 36. They ran three plays, got to fourth down and couldn’t convert.

5. The bye comes at a good time for WSU

Every coach in America will say the same thing about their team’s bye week: It comes at a good time. But it’s especially true for these Cougars, who will get an extra week to prepare for a home game against Colorado State, which harbors the worst defense in college football.

Theoretically, WSU shouldn’t need much help taking down such a lowly defense, but the Cougars also managed 20 points against an SDSU defense that had given up point totals of 41, 66 and 56. With a week off, look for Moore and the Cougs to make the adjustments they need to earn their first FBS win of the year.

Washington State.title: Dan Doornink, WSU hall of famer and longtime Seahawks running back, dies at 70
Washington State.summary:
Dan Doornink, a standout running back at Wapato High and Washington State University who then went on to an eight-year NFL career that included seven seasons with the Seahawks, has died at the age of 70, the Seahawks announced Sunday.

Doornink gained 1,836 yards with 15 touchdowns in 105 games for Seattle and may be best remembered for gaining 123 yards in a 13-7 wild-card playoff win over the defending Super Bowl champion Los Angeles Raiders at the Kingdome in 1984.

Doornink was affectionately known as “Dr. Dan” or simply “Dr.” for studying at the UW Medical School while playing for the Seahawks.

“I was competing against guys who didn’t have to study all the time,” Doornink once said in an interview with the Times. “It was hard and challenging and I didn’t get much sleep those years.”

After his NFL career ended he earned a Doctor of Medicine degree at UW and went on to a long career practicing internal medicine in Yakima.

Doornink revealed in 2021 that he had endured a long battle with COVID-19 that was made more difficult by a rare blood disorder. He said in an interview that year with the Seattle Times that he was in intensive care for 23 days and lost 38 pounds.

The team’s statement called Doornink “a beloved member of the Seahawks early days, both on and off the field.”

After a standout career at Wapato High, where the field is now named after him, Doornink recalled in a 2018 interview with the Seattle Times that he signed with WSU and then-coach Jim Sweeney as a quarterback. However, he was far down on the depth chart and moved to running back when injuries hit that position.

He led the Cougars in rushing in both 1976 and 1977, the latter season when WSU opened the season with one of the team’s biggest non-conference road wins ever, a 19-10 victory over 15th-ranked Nebraska. Doornink, a member of WSU’s Hall of Fame, remains 14th on the school’s all-time rushing list with 1,739 yards and is also 25th in career receptions with 105.

Taken 174th overall by the Giants in 1978, he rushed for 306 yards as a rookie despite missing six games with a shoulder injury before being traded to the Seahawks shortly before the start of the 1979 season for a 1980 seventh-round pick.

Doornink became a regular starter for the 1979 and 1980 seasons and then a key rotational player in the backfield from 1981-85. His 1,530 yards with the Seahawks is 14th in franchise history which included a career-high 500 in 1979 when Seattle finished 9-7.

He turned in his career regular season single-game high that season with 122 on 21 carries when the Seahawks beat Atlanta on what was the team’s first-ever appearance on Monday Night Football, a game many remember for Jim Zorn throwing a pass for a first down on a fake field goal to kicker Efren Herrera. That was the only 100-yard game of Doornink’s career in the regular season.

However, he would memorably top that number when Seahawks coach Chuck Knox decided to feature him as part of what was something of a surprise offensive attack emphasizing the running game when the Seahawks hosted the Raiders in the wild card round following the 1984 season. Seattle had lost its final two games against the Chiefs and Broncos, the latter contest costing the Seahawks the AFC West title, due in part to committing nine turnovers combined in the two defeats, including eight interceptions.

Knox decided to get back to basics against the Raiders, unveiling a double tight-end formation that the team used almost exclusively, and Seattle ran it 51 times while throwing just 10 in defeating LA. Doornink, who hadn’t had a carry in the previous two games, got handed the ball a career-high 29 times as the Seahawks took a 13-0 lead and held on.

“They knew exactly what we were going to do and still we were able to get th yards,” a happy Doornink said afterward.

Washington State.title: WSU hoops ready to kick off new season with home matchup against Davidson
Washington State.summary:
Earlier this summer, when David Riley was enjoying a break from coaching the Washington State’s men’s basketball team, he got a ribbing from his brother.

Noah Riley, a quality control coach and analyst for the NFL’s New York Giants, gave him a hard time: Our teams are way tougher.

Back then, Noah was likely referring to the two problems that have plagued Riley’s first two WSU teams: Turnovers and defense. The Cougars finished last season ranked No. 292 in turnover rate and No. 248 in effective field goal percentage defense, painting a picture of an undisciplined, mistake-prone club.

Ahead of Riley’s third season at WSU, which begins with a home matchup against Davidson at 6 p.m. Monday, can the Cougars reverse those trends?

“Well, I think it starts in practice,” said Riley, whose team plays just five home nonconference games this season. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

In the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU will use a retooled roster with 14 newcomers to try and turn around the problems that afflicted the last two Cougar teams. As they head into Monday’s season opener, they’ll likely start the same group that fueled their team’s second and final exhibition game, a road win over rival Washington last week.

That will likely mean lots of touches for East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who tallied a team-best 23 points and 11 rebounds in that game, plus opportunities for Central Missouri transfer guard Lazerek Houston and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips, each of whom scored in double figures. The rest of the Cougs’ starting lineup figures to include UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele and Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, whose size could make a difference for a WSU team that has struggled to rebound the past two seasons.

Against Davidson, which was picked to finish eighth of 14 teams in the Atlantic 10 preseason poll, WSU will likely need some more of that recipe. The Cougars played an ugly game to beat the Huskies . The game featured a combined 87 free throws, and neither team shot better than 40% from the field . But they did make nine 3-pointers. They got five combined from Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell and former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission.

From a 30,000-foot view, that’s the main contingent that the Cougars will use to replace several key offseason losses, including several to the transfer portal: Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. A few other names to watch include TCU transfer RJ Jones and French freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe.

Sankhe totaled five points and three rebounds in 15 minutes against UW.

Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins also figures to make a splash, but because an injury sidelined him for both exhibition games, it’s unclear when he’ll be able to get on the court.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons.”

Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO – Jaylen Thomas shook his head ever so slightly, almost imperceptibly so, as he thought about one of the problems holding back this Washington State team.

The Cougars had just turned in another loss, a 26-20 road setback to San Diego State on Saturday evening, and their secondary had just borne a fair share of the blame for this one. They are slogging through a considerable tackling issue, a key reason why the Aztecs ran wild on them.

“I just gotta find ways to get better at wrapping up,” Thomas said, “either taking the extra step to get closer to the running back. It’s just stuff I work on, just making sure I get the guy down as opposed to just making contact.”

SDSU racked up 202 yards and two touchdowns on 37 carries, including 115 from tailback Lucky Sutton, who broke free for several huge gains: a 46-yarder, two 11-yarders, a 16-yarder. His backfield mate, Javion Kinnard, scored two touchdowns on rushes of 9 and 10 yards.

The common denominator on those plays: The Cougars’ secondary, from Thomas to safety Jeremiah Bernard to nickelback Jamarey Smith, couldn’t bring down the Aztecs’ ballcarriers when they had the chance. They whiffed on several occasions, a problem that has sprung up lots of times this fall, most noticeably last week, when WSU missed 18 tackles in a loss to Boise State.

Give the Cougars credit for this: Their interior defensive linemen are making it difficult for opponents to run up the middle. Linemen like Kaden Beatty, Jirah Leaupepetele, Damarjhe Lewis and Paul Hutson have engineered that much, and they’ve done their job more often than not, using their hulking size and strength to deter Aztecs and Broncos, Bulldogs and Aggies.

So teams have wised up. San Diego State realized tailbacks had better chances going to the outside, which is true. That’s where Bernard and Thomas live, plus cornerbacks Jalil Tucker and Khamari Terrell, who are athletic and smart players. But they’ve been subject to bad tackling and some worse decision-making, choosing poor pursuit routes as they follow the ball.

“We had two goals going into the game,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said, “and the first one was to take care of the football and take the ball away. They’d won one game over three years when they lost the turnover battle. We didn’t do that. It was tied. Defensively, we wanted to keep them under 150 yards rushing. They rushed for 202. Did a better job of executing from that standpoint. There was a number of times to win the game outside of the last drive. Appreciate our players’ fight. We gotta go back to work.”

Here’s another trend that is holding back WSU’s defense: It can’t produce sacks. The Cougars didn’t bring down Aztec QB Stone Saunders for any sacks in this one, which might bely the pressure that defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk have generated with consistency, but they haven’t been able to finish those plays.

Headed into this game, WSU ranked No. 131 of 138 FBS teams with only eight sacks on the year. After the game, that number will stay the same. What has to change is the Cougars’ tackling ability, especially on the perimeter, if they want to earn one FBS win this season.

Washington State.title: How a few costly decisions set Washington State back in narrow road loss to San Diego State | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO – One day this winter, when this Washington State football season has come to a merciful end and coach Kirby Moore reflects on his first season with the program, he might sit in his office and ponder how it all went so disastrously wrong. And he might think about how at times, his Cougars were close to getting things right.

That was the case in WSU’s final game before the bye week, a 26-20 road loss to San Diego State on Saturday evening. In a game coming down to the final drive, Moore might wish he could have a few things back: the timeout he called on the Cougars’ final drive, the one he called before the Aztecs’ last touchdown, the decision to send out kicker Jack Stevens for a 53-yard field goal in spitting rain that fell hopelessly short.

When Moore contemplates it all, the reasons why the Cougars have spent the entire season to this point without an FBS win, he might wish for a do-over in several spots.

“We gotta learn how to finish – plays, drives, games,” Moore said after Saturday’s game.

The Cougars, 1-8 overall and 0-5 in Pac-12 play, did well to put themselves in a position to take the lead on their final drive of this game, a reality that reflects well on quarterback Owen Eshelman, who completed 30 of 42 passes for 299 yards and one interception that didn’t come back to bite him. The visitors’ defense also forced one turnover and forced a quick three-and-out to pave the way for that opportunity.

The Cougars reached midfield before a sack, a 5-yard penalty and two incompletions ended their hopes.

The majority of the rest of this loss, however, falls at the feet of Moore and his coaching staff. The list of costly decisions includes calling a timeout before SDSU’s final touchdown, which he said was at the recommendation of defensive coordinator Trent Bray, who didn’t like the look he saw. He called his team’s final timeout on its final drive, after a false-start penalty, to avoid a 10-second runoff. Earlier in the game, after Eshelman took a 10-yard sack, he sent out Stevens for a 53-yard field goal that never really stood any chance, thanks to the rain and wind.

Then, toward the end of the first half, WSU got the ball back with two timeouts and 50 seconds to go. The Cougars didn’t show much aggression at all, choosing to run the ball and kill the rest of the clock. Conditions weren’t exactly in their favor – Eshelman had just thrown his interception, and the rain made taking a shot risky business – but Moore and coaches have shown the same kind of dull approach in several other spots earlier in the season.

Besides, what does a 1-7 team have to lose? Too often, Moore has made conservative decisions instead of aggressively going for a win.

And on the timeout Moore called before SDSU’s trick-play touchdown: On fourth-and-goal from the 2, the Aztecs only needed a field goal to go up two scores. By going for it, they ran the risk of getting stopped short, leaving the door open for the Cougars to take the lead. They came out ready to go for it, which is when Moore called a timeout. What if SDSU had used that opportunity to think better of it and kick an easy field goal? That’s not what happened, of course, but that timeout gave SDSU a chance to make a better decision.

Here’s what Moore said about having zero timeouts for the final 74 seconds of the Cougars’ final drive, which ended on a turnover on downs when an Eshelman pass fell incomplete: “I think you’re still trying to just gain chunks. There’s pass opportunities there. Obviously, we gotta learn from, if no one’s open, we gotta be comfortable throwing the ball out of bounds and not taking a sack, and that’s one we definitely gotta learn from the next two-minute drive.”

Moore and his coaching staff bear even more of the brunt than that. The Cougs went 0-for-3 on fourth down in this one. Remember in the third quarter, when WSU decided to go for it on fourth-and-4 from the SDSU 30? Eshelman dropped back and couldn’t complete a pass to running back Kirby Vorhees. Give Moore credit for deciding to go for it in that spot, but that’s not the problem with that play.

Eshelman had to look for Vorhees in the flat because he got pressure pretty quickly, which happened because San Diego State utilized the same approach that Boise State did last week: a simple stunt. An interior Aztec lineman went inside and an edge rusher looped around to surge untouched into the backfield, hurrying Eshelman.

For WSU’s offensive line and coach Jack Abercrombie, it’s one thing to get beaten by that against Boise State, the class of the conference. It’s another to fall victim to the same approach a week later – to an SDSU defense that ranks among the nation’s worst.

Think about the defense WSU was facing in this one. Headed into Saturday’s game, San Diego State ranked No. 135 of 138 FBS teams in total defense (462 yards per game), No. 133 in scoring defense (36 ppg), No. 109 in rush defense (178 ypg) and No. 134 in pass defense (284 ypg). The Aztecs’ defense has given up 41 points to Toledo, 29 to Texas State, 66 to Oregon State and 56 to Colorado State.

So what prevented the Cougars from enjoying the same kind of success?

“The situational football piece,” Moore said. “We didn’t do a good enough job there in the red zone. We didn’t do a good enough job there on fourth down. Everyone’s got a piece of that, and obviously that starts with me.”

To their credit, the Cougs sustained several long drives on offense in this game, including series of 4:28, 4:59, 6:15, 6:25 and 4:05. They converted 9 of 14 third downs, a remarkable feat for a group that entered Saturday’s game ranked five spots up from dead last in the country in that department.

But this season, this group hasn’t been able to make the winning plays when they count most. These Cougars have been subject to the same kinds of problems all season long, like the fact that in Saturday’s game, their running backs combined for 34 yards on 14 carries. The same problems have vexed them all season, and while their offensive line should get some of that blame, the rest should go to their coaching staff, which has not been able to put their team in the best positions to succeed.

In fairness, Moore is a first-time head coach, and most people watching games on TV – or in person – are never privy to the hectic nature of games in which coaches make these decisions. It isn’t easy. But Moore is paid to learn these lessons, and in Week 9, it doesn’t appear that is happening.

Washington State.title: Nightmarish season continues for Washington State after loss at San Diego State | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
Washington State had a chance to pull off a fourth-quarter comeback on the road, but its final possession ended with a turnover on downs and the Cougars remained winless against FBS competition, falling 26-20 to San Diego State in a Pac-12 game on Saturday at a rain-soaked Snapdragon Stadium.

A nightmarish season continued for the Cougs (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12), whose offense couldn’t quite put a full game together against a woeful Aztec defense that entered the game among the worst in the FBS. WSU’s defense was effective against the pass. Against the run? Not so much.

Defensive cracks show

For the most part, WSU’s defensive front has been a strength of the team. The group made a few stops in big moments Saturday – notably, forcing a three-and-out on San Diego State’s final possession in the fourth quarter to give the offense a shot at a game-winning drive.

But overall, the Cougars’ defense was leaky against the run, surrendering 202 rushing yards on 37 carries for an average of 5.5 yards per attempt. The Aztecs had seven runs go longer than 10 yards, including a 46-yarder early in the game. Open-field tackling was a problem, as SDSU’s Lucky Sutton and Javion Kinnard churned through defenders for yards after contact.

SDSU recorded just 104 yards through the air and the Cougars tallied an interception, but WSU was fooled on a consequential pass, a WR trick pass play on a goal-line fourth down, which put the Aztecs up by 12 points midway through the fourth quarter. On that possession, SDSU leaned on the run to get into scoring position, moving the chains on Kinnard’s tackle-busting third-and-9 run to spark the important scoring drive, then picking up 16 yards on a Sutton run in the red zone that saw several WSU defenders whiff.

The Cougars’ rushing defense has been a weakness recently, allowing more than 200 yards in each of the past three games.

Offense can’t capitalize

The Aztecs entered the game ranked 133rd nationally (sixth from last) in scoring defense at 36.12 points per game and 134th in total defense (461.5 yards per game). No other defense in the nation had been on the field for more snaps (624) than SDSU’s this year.

For SDSU, it was apparently an ideal matchup against a WSU offense that ranks among the worst in the FBS.

Yet again, the Cougars made too many offensive mistakes and couldn’t run with their tailbacks (34 yards on 14 carries), spoiling what was a respectable effort from quarterback Owen Eshelman in his third start. He passed for a career-high 299 yards and rushed for two touchdowns, but threw an interception and was tagged with a third-down intentional grounding penalty in the red zone, which resulted in a missed field goal from long range.

Glaring issues emerged at the worst possible time, on WSU’s final drive with the team trailing by six points and with just under five minutes left. The Cougars couldn’t even reach midfield in 10 plays. The drive included two sacks and a false start, and ended with 38 seconds left, when Eshelman was hurried on fourth-and-10 and couldn’t complete a deep pass.

Managing only 20 points against an Aztecs defense that has proven to be more than susceptible is inexcusable for WSU and its offensive-minded head coach.

It’s gotten real gloomy

It started with so much hope – a promising new coach, a winnable new conference. But at this point, one has to wonder where this season might end up ranking among the all-time worst in WSU history.

At least the awful teams of years past were losing in a true power conference. These Cougars can’t contend against former Mountain West squads that WSU used to steamroll. It’s ugly. It’s a sad state. And it could get worse before it gets better – hopefully, it does, and this proves to be a building season. But right now, a one-win season is a real possibility. What would happen then?

Washington State.title: Washington State quarterback Owen Eshelman shows more progress | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
WSU QB Owen Eshelman

The Cougars’ redshirt freshman signal-caller made a couple of glaring mistakes – an errant pass that was picked off in the second quarter and an intentional grounding when WSU was in scoring position in the third – but was otherwise poised and continued to show progress in his third start. In the end, he fell just a few plays short of leading a fourth-quarter comeback. Eshelman rushed for two touchdowns and completed 30 of 42 passes for a career-high 299 yards.

SDSU RB Javion Kinnard

The sophomore transfer exhibited elusiveness and some power despite his 5-8, 175-pound frame. He kept his legs moving to pick up extra yards and shed Cougar tacklers, averaging 5.1 yards on 17 carries. Kinnard scored the game’s first TD, a 9-yard burst, and put the Aztecs up 14-7 early in the second quarter with a 10-yard scoring run on third down. He finished with 87 yards, complementing starting back Lucky Sutton, who tallied 118 yards on 18 carries.

Washington State.title: Complex or simple, Cougars have made head-scratching decisions | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
The Washington State Cougars have played nine games so far and won just one of them. There are many reasons for that but today let’s talk about decision making.

A beauty of football is that it is infinitely complex, and exceedingly simple. More often than not, the team with the bigger, stronger players has the advantage. Advantages are also gained by the team that has players who are faster, who can keep their speed while turning their hips more fluidly, who are born with some unknowable spatial genius and ability to perceive where a play is headed just an instant before everyone else.

Simple.

But of course, it is also very complicated. The plays and schemes employed by college football coaches require an amount of study that is probably analogous with many postgraduate degree programs. All but a few fans (and writers) only grasp a small portion of the variables happening in any given play call on either offense or defense, not even accounting for all the codes and cadences and other deceptions teams must employ to keep those play calls secret from the other team.

Some decisions made during a football game, however, aren’t that hard to understand. And those ones often seem to have the biggest impacts.

I don’t think WSU made very good decisions during the Cougars’ 26-20 loss to San Diego State, a very winnable game against a team that is also struggling.

Some of these head-scratchers were made by the players.

A field goal attempt to bring the Cougars within three points was made more difficult in the third quarter, when recently anointed starting quarterback Owen Eshelman avoided a sack by chucking the ball to no one, and not past the line of scrimmage, leading to an easy and obvious intentional grounding penalty.

On third down and well in field goal range, a sack was a bad result, but possibly not a decisive one. Tossing the ball to no one, however, had a high chance of leading to a grounding call, or worse, an interception.

Whether such snap mistakes are entirely the fault of players, or shared by coaches who are “allowing it to happen” is a debate that will never be settled. However, it does seem like situational awareness could use some emphasis throughout the program.

To begin the last drive of the first half, the Cougars trailed 17-14, and had 52 seconds and two timeouts with which to get into field goal range and head to halftime tied.

Instead they pocketed the timeouts, called a QB run, and called it a half. SDSU had the ball to start the second half, so the Cougars played it conservatively knowing they could be down two scores before touching the ball gain.

The coaches on the other side? Well, they called a double-reverse pass on fourth-and-goal up 20-14 early in the fourth quarter, rolling the dice and coming up 7. Well, six after failing the two-point conversion.

The game’s worst decision came when WSU coach Kirby Moore used his last timeout to save a 10-second runoff after a false start, with only 1:18 left in the fourth quarter. This drive began at their own 14-yard line with 4:43 remaining, and in three-and-a-half methodical minutes the Cougars had only plodded their way to their own 42-yard line.

To save 10 seconds, WSU gave away its ability to stop the clock after a deep completion that they would surely need to get in shouting distance of the end zone.

Did any of these miscalls cost WSU the game? Possibly not. But when you’ve got as many things going against you as the 2026 Cougars do, they shouldn’t be making things even easier for their opponents.

Washington State.title: Washington State's comeback attempt falls short | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO — The rain soaked Owen Eshelman’s uniform as he cruised into the end zone untouched, leaving him soggy and muddy. He had battled all night through the conditions, the mistakes, the listless possessions and the moments where his inexperience shone through like sunlight through a stain-glass window.

In this one, though, he looked like the spark plug the Cougars needed all along. He took a keeper a few yards into the end zone, releasing a scream as he did so, helping his WSU club draw within one score of San Diego State. For WSU, the complexion of the game had just changed in a bolt: It went from a forgettable eighth loss to a comeback with a dash of hope.

Moments later, though, coach Kirby Moore’s team suffered what has become all too familiar this season: A lack of winning plays when it mattered most, a key reason why the Cougars’ comeback fell just short in a 26-20 loss, the team’s sixth straight setback.

In the final moments of the fourth quarter, the Cougars (1-7, 0-5 Pac-12) earned the opportunity to complete a comeback by picking up a key stop on defense, forcing the Aztecs into a quick three-and-out. Just over two minutes elapsed on the clock, giving the Cougars back the ball with a shade under five minutes to play.

It’s the sixth straight loss for WSU, which is still looking for its first FBS win of the season in coach Kirby Moore’s debut campaign. It was a valiant effort from the Cougars’ offense, a source of frustration and confusion for fans and observers all fall, and a reminder that Eshelman is oozing potential. But in the end, it adds up to another setback.

In the fourth, San Diego State took what looked like a risky play and turned it into a sight to behold. On fourth-and-goal from the 2, the Aztecs could have gone up two scores with a chip-shot field goal. Instead, they went for it and scored on a trick passing play, seizing a 26-14 lead with about 10 minutes to play.

The Cougars’ defense had a hand in this loss, unable to tackle in space well enough to prevent some of the Aztecs’ biggest plays on the ground.

San Diego State opened the scoring early in the first quarter, capping a long drive with a touchdown rush from tailback Javion Kinnard, a nine-yard scamper into the end zone. That staked the hosts to a 7-0 lead.

WSU followed with its own long touchdown drive, which covered 75 yards and a hair shy of a full five minutes. It ended with a short keeper from Eshelman, who had just enough, reaching the ball across the plane for the last bit he needed. The Cougs tied the game at 7-all with that score.

San Diego State was quick to retake the lead, though, responding with a touchdown drive. Capping that was Kinnard, who jetted 10 yards into the end zone, good for a 14-7 lead.

Things continued to swing back-and-forth a drive later, which is when WSU tied the game once again.

Washington State gets its first and only bye of the season next week. Then the Cougars return to action on Nov. 14, hosting Colorado State at Gesa Field.

The Cougars were set up inside the five after a long completion to Daniel Blood.

The Aztecs’ 2-point conversion attempt fails.

3rd, 14:12 - SDSU 17, WSU 14: Jaylen Thomas intercepts SDSU QB Stone Saunders and the Cougars take over possession.

Eshelman throws interception

2nd, 1:49 - SDSU 17, WSU 14: Defensive end Kai Wallin intercepts Eshelman to give the Aztecs another possession before halftime.

Aztecs regain lead

Pregame

Washington State gets another crack at earning its first Pac-12 Conference and FBS win of the season, this time on the road against San Diego State.

Owen Eshelman and the Cougars’ offense should have room to operate after a tough game against Boise State last week.

The Aztecs (3-5, 2-2) are giving up about 36 points per game and allowing 462 yards per contest, some of the worst numbers nationwide.

For the WSU’s special teams, they will need to limit the threat of returner Jaylon Hawkins. The Cougar offensive line will also need to hold up against the Aztecs’ defensive front.

The game is scheduled to kick off at 4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network.

Series history

Washington State has won three of the four meetings between the Cougars (1-7, 0-4 Pac-12) and the Aztecs. 

Notatable stat

Washington State.title: How David Riley’s Washington State basketball team adjusted after another mass exodus last season
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – After David Riley wrapped up his second season at the helm of Washington State’s men’s basketball program in April, he may have felt like he was having deja vu.

For the second straight year, his entire starting five had departed. For the second straight year, he would have to rebuild an entire roster from scratch. He’d have to do it all via the transfer portal, which had claimed each of the top scorers from his first two WSU teams.

So headed into his third season, the Cougars’ basketball roster looks almost entirely brand new, as it has each of the two years that preceded it. Gone are Ace Glass and ND Okafor, two staples of last year’s WSU team, as are all but two players from that team.

Riley spent much of the spring and summer constructing the roster for this 2026-27 team, which kicks off its season Monday at home against Davidson, one of the rare nonconference games at Beasley Coliseum to open the season.

Before that happens, though, let’s revisit how Riley’s third WSU team came together, the players, the fits and how it all rounded into shape for the Cougars. The good news for Riley: In late March and early April, before the transfer portal officially opened, many of the WSU players who planned on leaving announced their plans to do so. The Cougars knew the players they would have to replace and had more time to scour the portal for new fill-ins.

That stands in stark contrast to last spring, when the players leaving WSU didn’t make that decision until after the portal opened, leaving coaches with less time to find their replacements.

WSU’s team includes 14 newcomers, including nine from the transfer portal: Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (D-II) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips.

Riley’s third roster also includes wing Casey Jones, who last played for Riley at Eastern Washington before taking the next two years off for a church mission, as well as Spanish guard Pedro Sancho Moraga, French forward Mohamed Sankhe Golden State Prep product Roman Stathis, freshman Brayden Kyman and returners Dominik Robinson and Dio Blakely.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us, trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said in late October. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons. I think we have more aggression, a little more confidence than last year.”

The Cougars’ first commitment of the offseason came courtesy of Roxburgh, who came over from Manhattan College in New York City, where he started in 31 of 32 games, averaging 11 points and 5.8 rebounds per game. Roxburgh also shot 44% from the field, including 32% from beyond the arc on four attempts per game.

He figures to play a stretch four role, not unlike that of former forward Simon Hildebrandt, who played for last year’s WSU team. In Roxburgh’s commitment, it became clear that Riley and coaches value some versatility at their small forward or power forward spots.

“I think when I was still at Eastern, we were looking at him more as a three-four,” Riley said in the spring. “He’s another guy who just brings a ton of versatility to the game. Can pass, can think the game.”

WSU coaches’ second addition of the offseason came from Houston, who lit up the Division II ranks last season, averaging 20.8 points, four rebounds and five assists on 46.2% shooting, including 37% from 3-point territory. A quick ball-handler and crafty finisher, Houston’s finalists included one of WSU’s future Pac-12 opponents, Boise State.

“On my visit, it kinda felt like a family,” Houston said. “Just talking to the coaches, it wasn’t awkward. I didn’t feel like I gotta portray myself as somebody else. I felt like I could be myself, talk to them, and I just felt like it was like a good community. And I wanted to be a part of that.”

Around the same time, Riley picked up commitments from two other players who figure to play cornerstone roles on this team, Akins and Harrison. Akins started his career at Denver before playing last season at Wake Forest, where he averaged 5.3 points in 15.2 minutes per game, starting in eight games.

Harrison started his career at Tarleton State before spending last season at East Texas A&M, where he averaged 14.7 points and 6.1 rebounds in 30 minutes per game, starting 28 of 30 games. He also shot an efficient 53% inside the arc.

“Ronnie is a guy that’s super talented,” Riley said. “Bigger than he looks on film. He came up on his visit, and just a big body, strong, really just a confident player that can do a little bit of everything.”

That’s also around the same time when Riley secured a commitment from Kropp, a transfer from Northwestern, where fans seemed disappointed to lose him. Starting 10 games that season, he averaged 3.1 points and 2.1 rebounds per game.

Other staples on this WSU team figure to include Phillips and Dembele, who joined Kropp, Houston and Harrison in the Cougars’ starting lineup for their exhibition opener, a 92-64 loss to New Mexico in October. Phillips profiles as a scoring guard, while Dembele provides some physicality underneath and some upside around the arc, where he can shoot it from 3.

Can that group help Riley put a forgettable season in the rearview mirror? It might help that over the offseason, his brother, Noah, gave David a hard time. “Our teams are way tougher,” Noah would say, referring to his New York Giants, where he works as a quality control coach.

Whether or not that’s true, what can David do to turn around that perception this season?

“I think it starts in practice,” Riley said. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

Washington State.title: David Riley, Washington State enter rebuilt Pac-12 with immense roster turnover
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When he looks back, David Riley realizes that in his first pair of years as Washington State’s head coach, he hasn’t let his players scrimmage each other in practice as much as he should have.

In those days, he ran his guys through all kinds of drills, all manner of concepts. That approach may have helped in its own right, but as Riley prepares for his third season with the Cougars, he wants to put players in more live situations. He wants to learn what makes each one tick, create more pressure situations.

After all, Riley figures, what happens if the first adversity WSU faces comes in its Nov. 2 season opener against Davidson?

“That’s a problem,” Riley said.

In their first season of the rebuilt Pac-12, the Cougars will try to avoid the ones that plagued them in their previous two years under Riley, whose teams couldn’t avoid turnovers or guard well enough. This year, with 14 newcomers and nine from the transfer portal, WSU has a chance to turn those around in a convincing way.

The Cougars opened the season with two exhibition matchups, a road loss to New Mexico and a road win over rival Washington, the latter of which can provide a window into how this team might operate. The key cogs in this group will involve East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, whose two-way acumen figures to make him a weapon on both ends of the court, as well as Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and Central Missouri (D-II) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, all of whom scored in double figures in their team’s win over UW.

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. Coaches had to hit the transfer portal to replace key players from last year’s team, including guard Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

So how will the Cougars’ new group mesh? That much will depend on Harrison, Phillips and Houston, as well as Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Northwestern transfer big man Tyler Kropp, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins and UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele. Former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission, is also back playing for Riley.

“There definitely is some differences when you have guys that have played in your system before and you know what’s returning, how to build around that,” Riley said. “For us, I think that’s the beauty of how we play. We’re pretty versatile. We’ve had teams that have been really good with guards, with bigs, with wings. I think being multidimensional is really important for us, and getting that physicality was something that we really wanted to embrace. I think we did that. Now it’s time to figure out how it all gels.”

The Cougars won’t get much of an easy on-ramp into the season. Including its season opener, a Nov. 2 home matchup with Davidson, WSU plays only four Division-I nonconference home games, the program’s fewest since the 1973-74 seasons. It highlights the way coaches like Riley have to keep the team budget in mind when building schedules, trying to generate revenue via buy games that can be used in a multitude of ways.

Here’s a sample of WSU’s nonconference schedule: at High Point on Nov. 7, at Duquesne on Nov. 10, against Duke in California on Nov. 21, at Murray State on Nov. 30, at Weber State on Dec. 9 and at LSU on Dec. 28. The Cougs will be away from Pullman more than this program ever has been since the ’70s. Couple that with the team’s new-look roster and you understand the challenges facing the Cougars.

And that’s to make no mention of the reimagined Pac-12, whose best sport might be men’s hoops. The Cougs will host No. 15 Gonzaga in early January, during their university’s winter break, and a February road stretch against Gonzaga and San Diego State will prove tough. WSU also has a road date with Utah State set up for late January. If it’s not a gauntlet, it’s something close.

It’s not easy for any team, let alone one like WSU, which has turned over its entire starting five each of the last two seasons.

“I’d say that was probably the biggest thing for us in the off-season – we had so many new guys,” Kropp said. “We just saw what a team like New Mexico with so many returners, how valuable it is and how valuable that chemistry is. That was just a big focus for us in the off-season. As soon as we got on campus, we made sure, as often as we could, whenever we had an off-day, we were together.”

To turn things around from last season, when the Cougars went 12-20 overall and 7-11 in their second and final season as West Coast Conference affiliate members, they will have to shore up two things most of all: Defense and turnovers. A year ago, WSU turned it over on about 18% of its possessions, which ranked No. 292 nationally. That group also allowed opponents to register an effective field goal percentage of 53%, which was No. 248 in the country.

So what’s the key to reversing those fortunes? Riley likes to say it involves identifying selfless players.

“I think that starts in the recruiting process, is getting guys who want to play this kind of basketball, who want to play a team style offensively and defensively, want to be physical and disruptive, and I think we did a good job of that,” Riley said. “We’re getting guys that understand the importance of that, and like I said earlier, I think once you really understand how we play, it’s impossible to do it alone.”

Washington State.title: Pac-12 preview: New-look conference should provide stiff challenges, hostile road arenas
Washington State.summary:
On Sept. 16, Utah State announced the school had sold out tickets for Gonzaga’s inaugural trip to Dee Glen Smith Spectrum. That wouldn’t necessarily be news – certainly not Gonzaga’s first time drawing a standing room-only crowd on the road – but the announcement arrived two full weeks before the Pac-12 Conference released its schedule, meaning more than 10,000 fans purchased tickets without knowing a concrete date for the Jan. 21 matchup.

Gonzaga can expect bigger crowds and more robust challenges in the new conference, which should test the Bulldogs top-to-bottom in a way the West Coast Conference didn’t and help Mark Few’s avoid the resume dings that were often inevitable in January and February.

The reimagined Pac-12 may not be ready to compete with the SEC, Big Ten, Big 12, ACC and Big East on Selection Sunday, but this new group of nine isn’t lacking credentials.

Gonzaga and San Diego State bring three combined national championship appearances over the last nine years with 31 combined NCAA Tournament victories sprinkled in during that span. Utah State is in the middle of the school’s best run, punching six NCAA tickets over the last eight seasons, including each of the last four. Boise State made three straight March Madness trips before recent misses and Colorado State has been exceptional in its own right, qualifying in 2022, 2024 and 2025. Oregon State and Washington State both made semirecent NCAA appearances under the Pac-12’s old flag.

This new-look Pac-12 might have been a candidate to get three teams into the previous NCAA Tournament, but the expanded 76-team bracket provides a pathway to one or two additional bids.

Regardless, college hoops fans out West should have plenty of dates to circle on the new Pac-12 calendar – not just the one taking place Jan. 21 in Logan, Utah.

1. Gonzaga

Coach: Mark Few (772-156), 28th year at Gonzaga

2025-26 record: 31-4. WCC: 16-2, tied-first

Key newcomers: C Massamba Diop (7-1, 230), G Isiah Harwell (6-6, 220), G Nathan De Sousa (6-2, 192), F Izan Almansa (6-10, 200/eligibility pending), G Xaivian Lee (6-4, 185), F Chauncey Wiggins (6-11, 225/eligibility pending), G Javon Bennett (5-10, 165/eligibility pending)

Key losses: F Graham Ike, G Tyon Grant-Foster, G Jalen Warley, F Emmanuel Innocenti, G Mario Saint-Supery, G Adam Miller, G Braeden Smith, C Ismaila Diagne

Outlook: Despite the various curveballs this offseason has tossed their way, the Zags are still the favorites – considerable favorites, maybe – to capture a Pac-12 crown next spring. They’ve assembled one of the country’s top frontcourts, blending Braden Huff’s offensive touch with Massamba Diop’s rim protection. This should be a second-weekend team with a Final Four ceiling if Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Chauncey Wiggins stay/become eligible.

2. Utah State

Coach: Ben Jacobson (397-259), 1st year at Utah State

2025-26 record: 29-7. Mountain West: 15-5, first

Key newcomers: Dallin Hall (6-4, 200/eligibility pending), Connor Turnbull (6-11, 225), AJ Bates (6-4, 200), Solomon Callaghan (6-2, 195), Will Hornseth (6-9, 235), Collin Mulholland (6-11, 240)

Key losses: G MJ Collins Jr., G Drake Allen, G Kolby King, F Garry Clark, F Adlan Elamin, G Elijah Perryman

Outlook: Constant coaching turnover hasn’t impacted the Aggies, who’ve been to four consecutive NCAA Tournaments under three different coaches. Utah State has a solid chance to get there again under Ben Jacobson, who made five NCAA appearances over 20 seasons at Northern Iowa. The Aggies will lean heavily on veteran forward Mason Falslev, the favorite to earn Pac-12 MVP honors if the award doesn’t go to a Gonzaga player. Frontcourt mate and reigning Mountain West Sixth Man of the Year Karson Templin is another solid all-conference candidate.

3. San Diego State

Coach: Brian Dutcher (220-79), 10th year at San Diego State

2025-26 record: 22-11. Mountain West: 13-6, second

Key newcomers: G Chance Gladden (6-4, 192), G Isaiah Sy (6-6, 200), F Bear Cherry (6-10, 270), G David Torresani (6-2, 168), G Zach White (6-5, 208), F Luca Vincini (6-10, 242)

Key losses: F Magoon Gwath, F Pharaoh Compton, G Miles Byrd, G BJ Davis, G Taj DeGourville, G Reese Dixon-Waters, F Miles Heide

Outlook: This won’t be Brian Dutcher’s strongest roster on paper, but we’ll give the benefit of the doubt to a coach who’s been part of four Mountain West regular-season or tournament championships and six NCAA Tournament appearances since taking over for Steve Fisher. Elzie Harrington, the team’s only returning starter, is a proficient 3-point shooter, but the Aztecs may also require a lot from transfers Chance Gladden (Boston U), Bear Cherry (Sacramento State) and Isaiah Sy (Oregon State), especially in the wake of Nick Anderson’s offseason knee injury.

4. Oregon State

Coach: Justin Joyner (0-0), 1st season at Oregon State

2025-26 record: 17-16. WCC: 9-9, tie-fourth

Key newcomers: F Jackson Rasmussen (6-9, 211), G Legend Smiley (6-5, 188), G Daniel Freitag (6-2, 192), F DeShawn Gory (6-6, 169), C Xavion Staton (7-1, 224), G Chris Johnson (6-5, 189), C Dennis Evans (7-2, 231)

Key losses: F Isaiah Sy, G Dez White, F Johan Munch, C Yaak Yaak, F Jorge Diaz Graham, F Olavi Suutela

Outlook: Justin Joyner, a national title-winning assistant with years of experience building scouting reports for Gonzaga, takes over Oregon State’s program after Wayne Tinkle’s tenure ended. Joyner lacks head-coaching experience, but he’s assembled a roster that looks talented enough on paper to compete with the top half of the Pac-12. Program veteran Josiah Lake II brings leadership and ball-handling, while transfers DeShawn Gory (Fresno State) and Daniel Freitag (Buffalo) have a chance to lead the Beavers in scoring. Similar to the Michigan team Joyner worked for last season, OSU should be massive up front with three 7-footers on this roster.

5. Colorado State

Coach: Ali Farokhmanesh (21-13), second season at Colorado State

2025-26 record: 21-13. Mountain West: 11-9, seventh

Key newcomers: G Justin Menard (6-3, 185), F Jaden Ghoreishi (6-9, 215), Amondo Miller Jr. (6-7, 195)

Key losses: F Brandon Rechsteiner, G Jevin Muniz, F Augustinas Kiudulas

Outlook: The Rams lose their top scorer from a year ago, but return players who ranked second, third, fourth, sixth and seventh in points per game. It’s a level of retention that’s hard to come by in the current college basketball climate and one of the primary reasons Ali Farokhmanesh’s group might be a step ahead of others in the Pac-12 when the regular season begins. Marist transfer Justin Menard slides into the starting lineup next to a quartet of returners that includes three double-digit scorers in Kyle Jorgensen (11.5 ppg), Carey Booth (10.7 ppg) and Josh Pascarelli (10.2 ppg). Spokane’s Jaden Ghoreishi could see minutes off the bench as a freshman.

6. Boise State

Coach: Leon Rice (336-189), 17th season at Boise State

2025-26 record: 20-12. Mountain West: 12-8, tie-fifth

Key newcomers: F Dovydas Butka (6-9, 225), G Ty Rodgers (6-6, 205), G Lamar Washington (6-4, 210/eligibility pending), G Damari Wheeler-Thomas (6-0, 190).

Key losses: F Javan Buchanan, F Drew Fielder, G Dylan Andrews, F Andrew Meadow, F Dominic Parolin

Outlook: Former Gonzaga assistant Leon Rice faces a tall task replacing Boise State’s four double-digit scorers from a year ago, especially after an offseason injury to Ty Rodgers sidelined the Illinois transfer indefinitely. Campbell’s Dovydas Butka is a nightly double-double threat while North Dakota State transfer Damari Wheeler-Thomas is expected to take on primary ball-handling duties. Returning reserves Julian Bowie and Aginaldo Neto both had 20-plus point performances in recent exhibitions against Idaho and Washington. If eligible, 5-in-5 Georgia Tech transfer Lamar Washington has a chance to be one of Boise State’s top scorers, rebounders and facilitators.

7. Texas State

Coach: Terrence Johnson (107-81), seventh season at Texas State

2025-26 record: 19-13. Sun Belt: 11-7, tie-second

Key newcomers: G Quel’Ron House (6-0, 180), G KJ Younger (6-4, 218), F Ronald Jessamy (6-8, 220), G Caleb Steger (6-5, 180)

Key losses: G Franck Emmou, G Jaelyn Lee, C Tay Knox, G Deke Thompson, F Isaiah Barganier, G Cameron Simpson

Outlook: DJ Hall is one of the best-kept secrets in midmajor basketball and should be at the top of every Texas State scouting report this season after averaging 15.6 points, 7.7 rebounds and 1.4 steals as a freshman. The Bobcats have continuity beyond Hall, though, and managed to bring back second-leading scorer Mark Drone (14.2 ppg), assists/steals leader Kaden Gumbs (3.0 apg, 1.9 spg) and guard Dimp Pernell, who made 40.6% of his 3-pointers before a season-ending injury. Southern Illinois transfer Quel’Ron House will have a chance to be one of Texas State’s top two-way players.

8. Washington State

Coach: David Riley (93-73), third season at Washington State

2025-26 record: 12-20. WCC: 7-11, eighth

Key newcomers: G Lazerek Houston (6-0, 155), F Ronnie Harrison (6-8, 210), F Fraser Roxburgh (6-7, 215), G Sebastian Akins (6-2, 175), F Ladji Dembele (6-8, 255), G Jaylen Harrell (6-5, 210), F Tyler Kropp (6-9, 230), G Jamari Phillips (6-4, 190), G R.J. Jones, 6-2, 189 (2.6 ppg, 0.4 rpg).

Key losses: G Ace Glass, G Rihards Vavers, F ND Okafor, F Eeemeli Yalaho, G Tomas Thrastarson, G Jerone Morton, F Emmanuel Ugbo, G Kase Wynott, G Adria Rodriguez, G Parker Gerrits.

Outlook: The Cougars lost 98.9% of their scoring from 2025-26 – only Dio Blakely’s 0.8 points per game return – and are easily the most challenging team to handicap a year later. With an all-new starting lineup and rotation, it’s wise not to read too deeply into WSU’s 92-64 exhibition loss at New Mexico, but also means David Riley’s squad could face growing pains through a challenging nonconference schedule that sends the Cougs outside of Pullman 11 times in November and December. Division II standout Lazerek Houston and East Texas A&M Ronnie Harrison both hit double digits on efficient shooting in the exhibition loss, with Harrison scoring 23 in Sunday’s 84-80 exhibition win at Washington.

9. Fresno State

Coach: Vance Walberg (33-80), third season at Fresno State

2025-26 record: 13-19. Mountain West: 7-13, 10th

Key newcomers: G Dragos Lungu (6-6, 180), G Ross Candelino (6-5, 198), F Bradey Henige (7-0, 240), G Brian Amuneke (6-5, 184), C Baye Fall (6-11, 205), G Quentin Rhymes (6-6, 195), G KJ Perry (6-3, 180)

Key losses: G Jake Heidbreder, F Deshawn Gory, F Jac Mani, G David Douglas Jr., C Wilson Jacques, G Zaon Collins, G Cameron Faas, C Gasper Kocevar, G Bastien Rieber

Outlook: Washington State and Fresno State face the biggest rebuilds and not surprisingly are the teams occupying the final two spots in our predictions. But there could be a sizable gap between the Cougars and Bulldogs, who are separated by 60 spots in Ken Pomeroy’s preseason ratings. Fresno State lost every contributor from last year and could rely heavily on guards Dragos Lungu, a 13.8 ppg scorer at UT Martin, and Ross Candelino, who averaged 11.2 ppg at Libscomb to lead them in the scoring column. The Bulldogs will have to turn things around after settling for a 19-45 record over Vance Walberg’s first two seasons.

Washington State.title: What WSU football needs to happen to beat San Diego State
Washington State.summary: Looking to earn its first FBS win of the season and end a five-game slide, WSU will need to exploit San Diego State's beleaguered defense.
Washington State.author: Greg Woods
