WSU’s Trey Leckner broke his foot twice in one year. He kept attacking his rehab
Washington State.summary: After months of rehab, Trey Leckner was back at square one this summer when he broke his foot a second time. Discouraged but determined, WSU's tight end returned by early October.
Washington State.author: Greg Woods

Washington State.title: WSU's keys to victory against San Diego State | 2-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State at San Diego State

Saturday, 4 p.m.

Line: SDSU favored by 2½

TV: CBS Sports Network Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU offensive line vs. SDSU defensive line: If anything became clear from the Cougars’ last game, a home loss to Boise State, it was this: WSU’s offensive line needs serious work. That group now faces an SDSU defensive front that has produced 16 sacks, including 8.5 alone from the linebacker trio of Djibril Rahman, Kai Wallin and Sione Hala. Defensive lineman Malachi Finau has also pocketed a pair of sacks.

How will the Cougars’ front five of left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell fare against that group? Last week against Boise State, they were responsible for two of the four sacks against QB Owen Eshelman, who was constantly under duress.

To properly cash in on the SDSU defense, which ranks No. 135 of 138 FBS teams in total defense (462 yards per game), No. 133 in scoring defense (36 points per game), No. 109 in rush defense (178 ypg) and No. 134 in pass defense (284 ypg), Eshelman will need time in the pocket.

How the Cougs win …

WSU also can win this game by reversing a couple trends on defense. The Cougars have dropped six interceptions, which is tied for the most in the country, and they’ve also generated only five turnovers, which is No. 126 nationally. Plus, they have only eight sacks, which is No. 131. For a defense that has generally played well, defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s group hasn’t been able to make key plays at key times.

Opportunities figure to be there for the WSU defense against the San Diego State offense, which is expected to start redshirt freshman Stone Saunders, who will be making only his second career start. He looked sharp in a loss to Colorado State last weekend, but he also threw a pick-six. Can WSU defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk create enough pressure to force a turnover?

How the Aztecs win …

San Diego State can win this one by doing what every FBS team has done against WSU this season: limit its offense. Quarterback Owen Eshelman has looked solid in his first two starts, but this will be only No. 3 for Eshelman, who threw a costly interception in a home loss to Boise State last weekend. The Aztecs might be able to deliver the same treatment by getting pressure on Eshelman in the pocket.

Plus, if SDSU can shut down WSU’s rushing game, the hosts will be in good shape. Running backs Kirby Vorhees, Leo Pulalasi and Maxwell Woods – the last of whom didn’t get a single carry last weekend – are averaging only 48 yards on 15 carries against FBS opponents this season. If the Aztecs can keep that trend going, look for them to come out on top.

Key stat: 3

That’s the amount of kickoff return touchdowns engineered by SDSU redshirt freshman wideout Jaylon Hawkins. He took one back 100 yards against FCS Portland State, one 96 yards against Texas State and one 97 yards against Oregon State. He’s been electric in the return game, and while the Cougs rank No. 16 nationally with only 16 yards per return allowed, they would be wise to keep Hawkins corralled.

Quotable

“Regardless (of) what the prize is or whatever that we’re playing for, I want to win. I know all the guys in the locker room want to win, and the coaches want to win,” WSU tight end Trey Leckner said. “So I think just the will to win. I think we have all the seniors, all the seniors that are still playing. We wanna send them out on a good note, and we wanna build momentum going into next year.”

Washington State.title: To knock off SDSU on road and earn first FBS win, WSU's offense will have to kick into gear
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – At the beginning of the week, when the frustration still hung in the hair like a bad smell and several questions lingered unanswered, Kirby Moore returned to what he knew for sure. As he thought back to Washington State’s last game, a home loss to conference power Boise State, he was certain of one thing.

In his second start at quarterback, Owen Eshelman may have thrown one critical interception, which is when the Cougars began to lose the lead and lose the game. But he also directed one scoring drive and kept things clean otherwise.

“I thought Owen battled his tail off,” Moore said.

If the Cougars play their best in their next game, a road matchup with San Diego State set for Saturday afternoon, Eshelman shouldn’t have to. That’s because WSU will be going up against one of the country’s worst defenses in SDSU, which ranks three spots up from last in the country in total defense and five spots up from last in scoring defense.

The Aztecs (3-5, 2-2 Pac-12) are giving up about 36 points per game, allowing some 462 yards per contest, some of the worst numbers nationwide. Looking to earn its first FBS win of the season and end a five-game slide, WSU (1-7, 0-4) would do well to take advantage of those trends.

Can Eshelman and the Cougars do so? That much will likely depend on a few factors: Can their offensive line protect Eshelman and clear space for a robust rushing attack? Can Eshelman avoid turnovers? And perhaps most importantly, what can WSU get out of its three-receiver rotation of Branden Ganashamoorthy, Daniel Blood and Tank Hawkins – and will Moore’s group expand things?

Receiver Darrius Clemons, who exited early from his team’s loss to Utah State earlier this month, is listed as questionable for Saturday’s game. In his absence, the Cougs haven’t exactly expanded their receiver rotation to include other pieces like West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees or walk-on Caleb Northcroft, who would likely be next up. Instead, Moore has asked even more out of his starters, especially Ganashamoorthy, who has played 503 snaps, the third most in the country among receivers. Blood has logged 448, which is No. 21.

WSU is one of only four teams with two receivers in the top 25, making clear what Moore seemed to indicate earlier in the week: Coaches really only trust those three starters. Is that conducive to a win, especially on the road? The temptation is to say no, but crazier things have happened.

“We talk about deliberate practice,” Moore said, explaining his use of only three wideouts. “That really starts with bringing great energy, having verbal combat, doing your assignment, making sure you’re not thinking out there, that you’re just reacting. I think we’ve had too many errors from a practice standpoint with guys (not) knowing their assignments, whether it’s motions, details within the position. We’ve got a lot of trust in the guys who are out there on the field. If other guys improve and they’re to the standard, they’ll be out there.”

Regardless of how that trend pans out, WSU will want more out of its offensive line, and it’ll be interesting to see whether Moore shakes things up at that position group. As currently constructed, the group of left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell aren’t just giving up sacks. They’re also struggling to run-block, which is making things exceedingly hard on the Cougs’ tailback trio.

Just how much has that limited the production of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi? In seven games against FBS competition, those running backs are averaging only 15 carries for 48 yards. They’ve enjoyed a stray long rush – against Utah State, Pulalasi broke free for a 52-yard touchdown jaunt – but more often, they haven’t seen any running lanes.

Could that change against San Diego State? Check out the patterns and the possibility seems to emerge. The Aztecs rank No. 109 nationally in rush defense, yielding an average of 178 rushing yards per game. Here’s the kicker to that, too: SDSU is allowing opponents to convert third downs at a 47% clip, which is No. 129 nationally.

That would be music to the ears of the Cougs, who are converting only 30% of their third downs, ranking six spots up from last in the country in that department. They’ve tried running up the middle to no avail. They’ve tried dropping back, which has often failed thanks to offensive linemen getting blown up. They haven’t found any easy answers.

Maybe they’ll get one this week in the form of the SDSU defense, which is a week removed from giving up a 50-spot in a 56-49 loss to Colorado State. The Aztecs have also been burned for 66 points against Oregon State, 41 against Toledo and 29 against Texas State, the last result a win. SDSU and third-year coach Sean Lewis have lost two of its last three.

Meanwhile, the Cougars will get a real challenge from the Aztec offense, which is prepared to start redshirt freshman quarterback Stone Saunders in place of Jayden Denegal, who ranks among the nation’s worst QBs in EPA per dropback. Last week against Colorado State, Saunders completed 23 of 33 passes for 369 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions, including a pick-six shortly before halftime.

But there’s another phase of the game that WSU will have to be sharp in: special teams. SDSU redshirt freshman receiver Jaylon Hawkins leads the nation with three kickoff return touchdowns, matching the single-season school record. He took one back apiece in games against FCS Portland State, Texas State and Oregon State.

The good news for the Cougars: They rank No. 16 nationwide in kickoff return coverage, permitting an average return of only about 16 yards. That should serve them well this weekend. If things go well for them, so it should for their quarterback, too.

Washington State.title: Why San Diego State will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – As the week unfolded, Washington State coaches and players said all the right things, trying to squeeze something encouraging out of a lost season.

They want to play for their 14 seniors, they said. They want to go out on the right note. They understand a bowl game is out of the picture, but they feel motivated by some of the circumstances around this year, coach Kirby Moore’s debut season.

So as WSU prepares for a road test against San Diego State, you can squint and see the Cougs pulling it off. But the rest of our eyesight foresees a win for the Aztecs, who have been sharp at home, going 3-1. The Cougars are 0-4 on the road.

Sometimes, it’s as simple as that. But the problems WSU has faced, like a leaky offensive line and a struggling running game, don’t figure to get solved in a week’s time. San Diego State’s defense ranks among the worst in the country in several departments, but its offense has covered for some of those mistakes.

Could the Cougars limit the Aztecs’ offense, especially considering that backup QB Stone Saunders will be making only his second start? Certainly. But WSU’s defense, as well as it has played, has not been able to cash out at key times. The Cougars have dropped six interceptions, tied for the nation’s lead, and they have only eight sacks, which is one of the worst figures in the land.

WSU gets a bye after this game, which will be music to the ears of the Cougs, who will have played nine straight grueling contests before getting a break. Here’s predicting they will need it.

Final score: San Diego State 34, WSU 24

Washington State.title: How a quiet spring allowed the Washington State women to focus on continuity
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – For Washington State women’s basketball coach Kamie Ethridge, the word continuity has a significant meaning this fall.

Two years removed from losing six players to the transfer portal and having to do a roster makeover, the Cougars welcome back all their starters and even a sixth who started 20 games.

The Cougars may not have the seasoning that Gonzaga’s returning five starters possess, but they believe there will be significant improvement in 2026-27.

Washington State showed it was heading in the right direction at the end of last season, winning four of its final five to finish 9-25 – the worst season under the ninth-year coach.

Ethridge and the Cougars are focused on wiping the sour taste of last year out of their mouths.

“I really feel good about this team,” Ethridge said. “The leadership of our older players has been unbelievably good.”

Ethridge spent less time in the transfer portal last spring, bringing in one player – 6-foot-2 sophomore forward Elizaveta (Lizzie) Filchagina, who spent a year at SMU.

The quiet spring was a respite considering the chaos that was created with six departures the year before.

“Now it’s so much about, can you get buy-in from your team and can you get players who are willing to just really live in the process,” Ethridge said.

Ethridge said it will be interesting to see how the new 5-in-5 eligibility format plays out. In the past, coaches used redshirt seasons to allow new, raw players time to adjust and develop. Now the eligibility clock is running as soon as freshmen arrive on campus.

Players on rosters before the eligibility change get an extra year if they haven’t used a redshirt season previously.

“The process may mean you don’t get to play much your freshman year,” Ethridge said. “The fear is still out there that they’re not gonna wait and they’re gonna be impatient and they’re gonna leave after one year when they don’t get exactly what they want. So it’s still so much about, can we prove ourselves as coaches and as a program and that we really show we can develop players and that they’re getting better year after year.”

Ethridge has a different recruiting strategy, panning for players internationally. Nine of 12 players on WSU’s roster are internationals. It has become a more attractive avenue to find players because of the name, image and likeness element.

She has no problem paying players within reason after they have proven their value. And if WSU can’t match what players may acquire elsewhere then the door is open for them to do so.

Ethridge wants players who buy into her culture.

“We have to make sure our culture is growing in a real positive way to make sure people want to be in this program,” Ethridge said.

Player retention in the offseason tells Ethridge her program is headed in the right direction after the hiccup two years ago.

Two of WSU’s three seniors arrived as freshmen – guard Eleonora Villa from Lissone, Italy, and post Alex Covill from Missoula. The third senior, guard Mackenzie Chatfield, transferred from Western Kentucky last year. Her eligibility is over after this season because she used a redshirt after enrolling at WKU from Auckland, New Zealand.

WSU brought in three freshmen, one from Belgium and one from Argentina, and one from Oregon. A redshirt freshman hails from France.

Sophomores Malia Ruud, from Pasco, and Tanja Valancic, from Slovenia, arrived last year and earned starting time. Sophomore Malvina Haziri (Kosovo) saw limited minutes last year.

The lone junior, Charlotte Abraham (France), started last year.

The Cougars have commitments from two more internationals in the class of 2027. Ethridge continues to tap into that pipeline, something she hopes will serve WSU well in the rebuilt Pac-12.

Washington State.title: Washington State women ready for bounce-back season in new Pac-12
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Kamie Ethridge expects her Washington State University women’s basketball team to be much improved in 2026-27.

Whether that’s enough to put a 9-25 record last year in the rearview mirror remains to be seen.

Count senior point guard Mackenzie Chatfield as one thoroughly motivated by what transpired a year ago.

When asked what drove her during the offseason, Chatfield cracked, “Losing 30 games. That probably hit me really hard.”

A slight exaggeration but point well made.

“Last year was last year,” Chatfield said. “I have to be better for this group, be better for my teammates. We were here all summer and we grinded it out together. Knowing that this is my last year and I only have one more shot at it, I’m gonna give it my all no matter what.”

Chatfield said being with this team makes it easy to want to change things.

“You want to go to war with these girls, and they’re so capable of great things,” Chatfield said.

Including Chatfield, who transferred from Western Kentucky last year. But a strange thing happened to her near the end of her time there. She lost all confidence in her 3-point shooting – not because of a fundamental flaw in her shooting touch but because of a shoe that caused nerve damage to a foot, Ethridge said.

Chatfield made 28 of 80 shots behind the 3-point line (35%), but she only attempted one last season for the Cougars.

She spent the offseason retraining herself.

“It’s something that I have worked really hard on,” Chatfield said. “It’s all mental. Like when you’re able to do something in your sleep and you can’t do that again and then you have to try to relearn something. I don’t know how many hours me and Laurie (Koehn, assistant coach) have spent together. So just trusting the process and trusting the work. I don’t want that to be solely what I’m capable of. I want to still be able to play in multiple ways.”

She averaged 4.6 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.3 assists per game. Those are numbers that should increase measurably this season.

Chatfield will have lots of help. The Cougars return all five starters and a sixth when counting Malia Ruud, who had 20 starts as a true freshman last year.

Senior guard Eleonora Villa, an All-West Coast Conference second-team pick, led WSU with 16.5 points. Senior Alex Covill, who missed 14 games dealing with a foot injury, averaged 10.8 points and 4.5 rebounds.

At 6-foot-6, Covill will be expected to have more of a scoring presence inside and on the boards.

The other returning starters are junior guard Charlotte Abraham (10.3 ppg, 6.2 rpg) and sophomore forward Tanja Valancic (3.3 ppg, 3.2 rebounds), who started 25 games.

Ethridge is thankful for the experience.

“It’s amazing what a year forward means,” Ethridge said. “There’s a lot of comfort in the older players. All the older players got better and I feel very secure about them.”

The biggest question marks are among the six new names to the roster. Most of the new blood comes in the form of three freshmen – four when including a redshirt freshman.

The four freshmen and two sophomores, including 6-2 SMU transfer forward Elizaveta (Lizzie) Filchagina , will battle for minutes off the bench.

Ethridge has noticed three specific things in preseason practices that are encouraging.

“We are a little more balanced,” she said. “We are a little more physical than we’ve been in years past. We communicate better than we have in the past.”

Still, Ethridge knows consistent offense will cure a lot of ills.

“It’s still a shot-making game and a decision-making game,” Ethridge said. “We are really good some days and maybe not as good other days.”

Villa and Covill will command much attention from opponents. Villa scored a career-high 560 points last season, reaching double figures in 30 of 34 games.

Covill, who has struggled with injuries throughout her career, says she’s healthy and ready to go.

“We have learned a lot of lessons from the years before, especially last year, and the returners have come into this year wanting to change some things and create a new dynamic,” Covill said. “And we’re thankful we have newbies coming in as well. They’re following along and want to work hard and get better every day.”

Said Ethridge: “It’s (early). With the pieces that we have, we have a chance to be pretty good in January, February. But we’ve got to grow them fast and need everybody bought in and believing in what we’re doing here.”

Washington State.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Washington State.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Washington State.title: At home, San Diego St. will likely give WSU fits and a Mike Leach-inspired coaching list | Week 9 picks
Washington State.summary:
Welcome to the Hotline’s weekly picks against the point spread, published Thursdays throughout the regular season with a focus on the most intriguing matchups across the West and the top games nationally. Betting lines are courtesy of VegasInsider.com unless noted otherwise. (Games involving FCS teams not included.) I went 5-6-1 last week and am 50-46-3 for the season (52.1%). Picks are for entertainment purposes only … unless they aren’t.

The only thing better than watching a stacked Saturday of college football is watching a stacked Saturday of college football and then indulging in the leftover Halloween treats.

The Hotline has always favored chocolate bars but acknowledges the merits of the hard and chewy candies. The late, great Mike Leach was onto something when he spoke glowingly about Nerds Clusters during a post-game interview.

With that in mind, allow us to present college coaches as Halloween candy:

Arizona’s Brent Brennan: Snickers. If the coordinators (Seth Doege and Danny Gonzales) are the peanuts and caramel, Brennan’s the chocolate that makes it all work at an elite level.

Arizona State’s Kenny Dillingham: Skittles. Relentless energy and extremely popular with the younger generation.

Boise State’s Spencer Danielson: 100 Grand. Highly underappreciated and, in our view, one of the very best.

BYU’s Kalani Sitake: Milky Way. Somewhat old school, impossible to dislike and deserving of more support from its manufacturer.

Cal’s Tosh Lupoi: Tootsie Rolls. Tough at first but worth the wait (or so Cal fans better hope).

Colorado’s Deion Sanders: Candy Corn. Perhaps the most polarizing candy on the market and, some would say, past its prime.

Oregon’s Dan Lanning: Reese’s Mini Peanut Butter Cups. Lanning has lost more than 20 pounds this fall due to stress but remains very, very good.

Oregon State’s JaMarcus Shephard: Starburst. A rising star in the coaching industry who … wait for it! … has burst onto the scene.

Stanford’s Tavita Pritchard. Nerds. Duh.

UCLA’s Bob Chesney: M&Ms. Always good, regardless of circumstances or location, in all flavors.

USC’s Lincoln Riley: 3 Musketeers. Looks impressive on the outside but all fluff in the middle. (This is so obvious that, frankly, the comparison feels a tad trite.)

Utah’s Morgan Scalley: KitKat White Creme Wafer. Delicious new version of an absolute legend with distinctive layers.

Washington’s Jedd Fisch: Smarties. Like the man who has worked for 12 teams in the past 20 years, Smarties don’t last long.

Washington State’s Kirby Moore: Butterfinger. We aren’t sure what to make of it.

To the picks …

Cal (+7) at NC State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ACC Network

Comment: The Bears are flying across the country for a second consecutive week but will face an opponent that 1) just lost to Stanford and 2) just fired its coach. No way the Bears get overrun in Raleigh by a leaderless opponent, despite how poorly they have played most weeks. Pick: Cal

Arizona (+31/2

) at Texas Tech

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Wildcats recently walloped the team (Cincinnati) that thumped the Red Raiders just last week. Although the locations have changed, the trends will stay the same: Texas Tech is worse than advertised; Arizona is better than advertised; and the visitors have Noah Fifita. Pick: Arizona

Stanford (+221/2

) at Louisville

Kickoff: 12:15 p.m. on ACC Network

Comment: The Cardinal (color) have lost three road games by 133 points. The Cardinals (bird) aren’t in the same class as Wake Forest or Notre Dame, which hung 50-burgers on Stanford. But they are close enough to that level to win handily. Pick: Louisville

Florida (+111/2

) vs. Georgia

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on ABC

Comment: The Cocktail Party has been moved indoors, to Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium, because of facility renovations in Jacksonville. We think the Bulldogs, who had two weeks to stew over their loss to Auburn, will use this as the proverbial get-right game. Pick: Georgia

Arizona State (+16) at BYU

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Fox

Comment: For all the improvement the Sun Devils displayed last weekend against Kansas State, their two shortcomings – wobbly quarterback play and limited physicality – are more problematic in Provo than perhaps anywhere else in the Big 12. Also, the Cougars will be ornery after the loss at UCF. Pick: BYU

Northwestern (+31/2) at Oregon

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Peacock

Comment: Based on how the teams have played in recent weeks, the Wildcats should be favored. Anytime betting lines make absolutely no sense, we take note. Chip Kelly’s return to Eugene, as Northwestern’s playcaller, won’t be enjoyable. Pick: Oregon

Utah (-61/2

) at Cincinnati

Kickoff: 12:45 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: Fascinating offsets here: Yes, Utah is making the long trip after a taxing win (over Houston), but the Bearcats are coming off an upset of Texas Tech and the subsequent field-storming. If those factors cancel each other out and we’re left with tactics and personnel as the determinants, the advantage swings to the Utes. Pick: Utah

Purdue (+71/2

) at Penn State

Kickoff: 1:15 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: This matchup jumped off the VegasInsider.com screen because the line is something out of a bygone era. The Boilermakers no longer stink, but the Nittany Lions do. Pick: Purdue

Washington St. (+21/2

) at SDSU

Kickoff: 4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network

Comment: The Aztecs have been bad on the road but solid at home; the Cougars have been awful everywhere. If the hosts get to 17, they should cover … handily. Pick: San Diego State

Ohio State (-61/2

) at USC

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on NBC

Comment: How will the Trojans respond to their dreary performance at Wisconsin? Fairly well, we suspect. How will the Buckeyes perform without quarterback Julian Sayin? That’s far from certain. Sure, they have No. 4 (Jeremiah Smith), but someone has to get him the ball often enough for the nation’s best player to make an impact. Pick: USC

Washington (+71/2) at Nebraska

Kickoff: 5 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: The Huskers pushed Indiana to the brink a few weeks ago. But if Washington’s quarterback play (Demond Williams or Elijah Brown) is free of turnovers – that’s a big ask, from what we have seen lately – this should be competitive throughout. Pick: Washington

Texas St. (+111/2

) at Boise St.

Kickoff: 7 p.m. on the CW

Comment: Texas State’s wobbly defense is no match for the Broncos’ balanced, relentless offense. Close early. Not close late. Pick: Boise

Oregon St. (-6) at Fresno St.

Kickoff: 8 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: Are the Beavers a true steamroller? Did they spend too much time during the bye week basking in the accolades? This is their toughest test since facing Texas Tech in Week 2. We see a few speed bumps but no barricades. Pick: Oregon State

Straight-up winners: California, Arizona, Louisville, Georgia, Brigham Young, Oregon, Utah, Purdue, San Diego State, Ohio State, Nebraska, Boise State and Oregon State

Five-star special: Oregon State. In a difficult environment, the Beavers will prove they are a worthy challenger to Boise State in the Pac-12 and a legitimate contender for the playoff.

Washington State.title: Inside WSU TE Trey Leckner's injury rehab and how he's made an impact in four games back
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The reaggravation amounted to the worst days. Trey Leckner had missed all of spring ball with a foot injury, and as he angled to return as Washington State’s top pass-catching tight end, he had every reason to believe he could enter his final form in his redshirt junior campaign.

Then, over the summer, he broke his foot again. He would miss the entirety of fall camp with the injury.

“That was really hard,” Leckner said.

In all, Leckner was out almost the entire calendar year: spring ball, summer workouts, fall camp, the beginning of the season. He was expected to miss the first half of the Cougars’ 2026 campaign, which would have meant a return in mid-October, a costly blow for an offense that would prove to be anemic. But Leckner recovered quicker than anyone in the building expected. His first game back came on Oct. 3, in WSU’s home loss to Fresno State.

Since then, Leckner has caught 12 passes for 92 yards, including four-reception outings against Utah State earlier this month and Boise State last weekend. That hasn’t led to wins – not much has this season for the Cougars, who are still looking for their first FBS victory – but with his reliable hands and shifty athleticism, Leckner has given new quarterback Owen Eshelman a handy release valve in tight spots.

The best example came late in the second quarter, midway through the long scoring drive that WSU used to tie the game before halftime. Facing a fourth-and-2 near midfield, the Cougars needed a play to net them a couple yards. It probably wouldn’t come on the ground, where their offensive line has struggled to clear space for their tailbacks. And a standard shotgun dropback pass didn’t seem like a smart idea either.

So WSU coach Kirby Moore looked at his playsheet and dialed up a short pass from Eshelman to Leckner. In only his second career start, the Cougars’ redshirt freshman quarterback took a quick dropback and laced a pass to Leckner, who had come surging to the right while the rest of his teammates flowed to the left. That meant Leckner was wide open, and after he caught the ball, he only needed to fall forward another yard or so for the first down.

Ten plays later, WSU running back Kirby Vorhees squeezed into the end zone and the game was tied at 7-all.

“Obviously I was coming back across the field and I saw the D-end rush up the field,” Leckner said, “so I snapped my eyes around quick, and I knew it was gonna be coming to me on fourth-and-short. So just put my head down and tried to get the first down. And it’s been great playing with Owen. I mean, I think he’s a really good leader. I think since he’s taken over the role, he hasn’t flinched. He hasn’t shown any nervousness or anything like that. So it’s been really good to play with him.”

It’s tricky business, discussing any encouraging developments with this WSU offense, the unit that ranks among the country’s worst in just about every department you like. The Cougs are scoring only 1.35 points per drive, which ranks No. 135 of 138 FBS teams, a niche stat that does a nice job of painting the whole picture: As Eshelman takes over for Caden Pinnick, he’s looked far sharper and accurate than his predecessor, but many of the same problems exist with this group.

Washington State still can’t run the ball, averaging only 15 carries for 48 yards from running backs in seven games against FBS competition. The Cougs’ offensive line still can’t clear lanes for those guys, and they still can’t keep their quarterback clean. And even with Moore calling plays, which he has now done on a full-time basis for the last three games, nothing consistent and explosive has washed over their offense.

That forces you to look at the details, at the finer points with this offense that could help WSU take down San Diego State on the road this weekend. Can the Cougars end their five-game losing streak? They’ll be going up against one of the country’s worst scoring defenses in the Aztecs, who rank No. 135 in total defense (462 yards per game) and No. 133 in scoring defense (36 points per game).

Can Leckner make an impact against that type of defense? The temptation is to say yes. He’s fluid and reliable. In 13 targets this year, he has 12 receptions, and he has yet to drop a pass. In fact, in his entire career, he has been dinged for only one drop, which came in last winter’s Idaho Potato Bowl. Add it all up and you get these numbers: 52 targets, 41 receptions, 365 yards, four touchdowns, and just one drop.

He’s doing it all as a bit of a tweener, listed at 6-foot-3 and 243 pounds. He’s not enormous and burly like other tight ends, but he’s also not tiny, either. He’s also carving out this type of career at WSU, which isn’t exactly known for producing prestigious tight ends, at least not in the modern era. Back in 2017, the late Mike Leach was quoted as saying, “God didn’t make very many true tight ends.”

Leach may not have used tight ends in his time at WSU – in fact, he was famous for refusing to use them at all – but they’ve enjoyed something of a renaissance in recent years, especially in Pullman. Leckner has helped facilitate that, as has former Cougar Cooper Mathers, who set the program’s single-season record for touchdown catches by a TE with six during the 2024 season.

So how did Leckner become a tight end in the first place? Back in high school, at Glacier Peak in Snohomish, he remembers feeling like he was too slow to be a receiver, but a bit too big to play running back. “So tight end, kinda H-back was that perfect spot for me,” Leckner said, “where I can do everything, kinda be a Swiss Army knife in the offense.”

Leckner has been all of that and more for WSU. Among Cougars who have at least 75 pass-blocking snaps, he ranks tops on the team with a Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of 69. In the run-blocking department, he checks in with a grade of just 45.3, which is far below average.

Can that number be chalked up to the possibility that he’s still working his way back into shape? Maybe, but he’s finished with similar numbers in each of his previous two years – 48.5 in 2024, 56.1 in 2025 – so it’s more likely he’s just more of a finesse player.

That has served him well. So has his drive to get back on the field. Earlier this year, when he was working through rehab to do so, he impressed tight ends coach Derham Cato, who has been coaching for more than 15 years. Sometimes when a player is working his way back from injury, he said back in August, he worries about them losing “that mental intensity.”

“But that has not been the case,” Cato said. “He’s still got his notepad out every meeting. He’s taking notes. He’s dialed. He’s right behind with the guys that aren’t on the sideline every team period, talking to them, right? Just in terms of technique stuff, scheme stuff, responsibility stuff. So he’s done a hell of a job with it.”

“I’m definitely the type of person where it’s everything or nothing,” Leckner said. “I think, yeah, I have to knock the rust off. Obviously, missing all spring and all fall camp and getting back into the swing of things. I’m definitely still making mistakes that maybe I wouldn’t have made – you know what I mean? – if I had all that time practicing and getting better. But just working the new techniques with my coaches and really just grinding, grinding in practice, so I can go out there and execute.”

Washington State.title: Dropped interceptions and whiffed sacks: What's been missing from WSU's defense this fall?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Matyus McLain might be the happiest guy on Washington State’s team. He smiles everywhere he goes, from the practice field to game settings to press conferences, greeting everyone he sees with a warm grin and a delighted demeanor.

As the Cougars slog through this season, carrying around a 1-7 record as they continue searching for their first FBS win, it registers as remarkable. How does McLain, one of the team’s top defensive ends, stay in such a good mood?

It helps to know a bit about McLain’s background. He hails from nearby Priest River, Idaho, where in high school, McLain won a total of two games in his four years of action. The Spartans went 0-8 in 2019 and 0-7 in 2020. In 10 of those losses, Priest River didn’t score. In 2021, the Spartans lost seven games, only winning one by forfeit over Orofino. Priest River went on to win two games in McLain’s senior season, including one over the same Orofino club that had forfeited the year prior.

“I’ve lost before. It happens,” McLain said earlier this week. “The only thing you can do is keep going. I’m not gonna roll over and quit, and I don’t think anybody else in the locker room is going to do that either. You see the same thing week in, week out. We’re gonna keep trying harder and harder every single week till we get it right.”

McLain’s attitude is particularly fascinating because among these Cougars, he might have some of the most reasons to feel frustrated. Over the winter, he transferred from FCS Idaho, looking to use his speed and power to generate sacks for WSU. He looked like a candidate for a breakout year. All the signs were there.

In eight games, McLain has delivered on some of that promise. He has produced 23 quarterback pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, which is third in the Pac-12. He has also engineered a win rate – which measures how often a defender beats their blocker within 2.5 seconds of the snap – of 17.1%, which is also third in the conference. He’s faced few issues getting into opposing backfields.

But when he’s gotten there, McLain hasn’t been able to bring down quarterbacks. He has only one sack to his name. His fellow edge rusher, Vanderbilt transfer Linus Zunk, has only two sacks on 17 QB pressures. As a team, WSU has collected only eight sacks, which is tied for No. 130 of 138 FBS teams. Only four other teams in the country have supplied fewer.

If that sounds rare, it’s because it is. In college football, 71 players have totaled at least 20 QB pressures, according to PFF, including McLain and Zunk. Only five have generated one sack or fewer.

For WSU, it’s been a disappointing string of results, but it also presents a contrast that’s difficult to square: The Cougs are producing all kinds of pressures on quarterbacks, but they aren’t completing those plays with sacks.

That folds in nicely with the bigger issue with WSU’s defense: The group is having trouble getting turnovers. The Cougs have nabbed only five, which ranks No. 126 nationally. Only seven other teams have fewer turnovers. It hasn’t been a back-breaker for WSU, whose defense is still a plus, but that group is now allowing nearly 387 yards of offense per game – No. 102 nationally, fifth in the Pac-12.

“Our coach, Andrew Browning, he always talks about it: We’re not chasing sacks,” McLain said. “We’re chasing hits, hurries. Chasing that, it’s gonna lead to sacks. I mean, you’re right. (It’s about) getting there a little faster, but you watch the tape – we’re all over the D-line. The front seven is everywhere. No question about it. We’ve got it.”

For WSU, the part that might sting most is that defenders have had chances to bring down quarterbacks, to grab interceptions. In the third quarter of a loss to Boise State last weekend, the Cougars had a chance to do two things: bring down BSU QB Maddux Madsen for a sack, plus get off the field on third down. If they did that, they would have had a chance to take the lead.

Instead, Madsen eluded the pressure and dashed upfield for a 17-yard gain, which led to a touchdown moments later. In hindsight, it was the kind of sequence that sums up this entire WSU defense’s season: some encouraging flashes and serious potential, but it didn’t land.

In the same game, the Cougs had a few chances to intercept Madsen, who still has not thrown one this fall. One came toward the end of the first half, not long after WSU and QB Owen Eshelman turned in a long scoring drive to tie the game, when Boise State marched into the red zone. Madsen dropped back and laced a pass over the middle, where WSU nickelback Jamarey Smith broke on the route, but BSU receiver Cam Bates got a hand in the mix to prevent Smith from catching it.

Earlier in the game, back in the first quarter, Madsen tried a pass over the middle, where WSU linebacker DJ Warner was waiting. He reached out and got two hands on the ball, but it fell incomplete. It was a missed opportunity for Warner, who in his first year playing linebacker is still learning the ropes of the coverage side of his job.

Consider this stat: The Cougars have now dropped six interceptions, which is tied for the most in the country. Smith has dropped three, which is the second-most by one player nationwide.

You can read that number a couple of ways. Sometimes, a low figure might mean that defenders are simply capitalizing on their opportunities to make interceptions. Other times, it means that defenders aren’t in position to grab interceptions in the first place. There’s plenty of context involved.

For their parts, the Cougs have collected three interceptions, so they’ve taken advantage of several chances. But they’ve also dropped six, and in a 1-7 season, that figure looms large.

“We’ve definitely been in that position numerous times, and it’s all about, like I said, just executing,” Smith said. “When you get that chance and opportunity, just take it. You work so hard for it, so why not just go for it and take your shot? I’ve been there for sure, and it’s just about us having it and executing.”

Washington State.title: Cougars Head to San Diego State for Halloween Matchup
Cougs In Pro Basketball | October 27, 2026
During a 1-7 season, what keeps WSU players motivated to keep playing?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Trey Leckner admits that when he was younger, years before he began to flourish as Washington State’s premier pass-catching tight end, the noise could get to him sometimes. He was in high school, at Glacier Peak over in Snohomish, and he internalized some of the criticism.

That type of noise doesn’t bother him much these days, he said, in large part because of the journey it took for him to arrive at WSU. He redshirted his true freshman year in 2023, then began to ascend toward the back half of the following year, then earned a starting role in 2025. He missed the first four games of this season, his redshirt junior campaign.

When you watch him play, you wouldn’t know it. He caught a key fourth-down conversion over the weekend, in WSU’s 31-10 loss to Boise State, giving him these numbers in four games: 12 catches for 98 yards, including an 18-yard reception. He’s been the same kind of downfield threat that made him such an enticing prospect years ago.

“I think just getting older and being in the locker room,” Leckner said earlier this week, “being around a lot of really good players, obviously through 2023 and on. Just picking their brain and having good mentors, whether it’s players or coaches. Just being around it for so long.”

Leckner’s veteran presence is surely coming in handy this season, a 1-7 campaign for WSU, which is still looking for its first FBS win of the season. Head coach Kirby Moore and the Cougars had few issues cruising past FCS Duquesne in mid-September, but since then, they’ve dropped five in a row.

They’ve tried changing playcallers. They’ve tried changing quarterbacks. The Cougs’ offense has enjoyed some improvement since Moore benched Caden Pinnick for Owen Eshelman at quarterback, but in two games with that move, it hasn’t resulted in wins for WSU.

The only sure thing this WSU season has yielded is criticism: from fans, from media, from college football observers at large. The Cougs’ is a high-profile program, even in their new era within the reimagined Pac-12, which means they hear about it when things are going as poorly as they are now. They may sign up for it when they agree to such a platform, sure, especially when they accept such big paydays in the new name, image and likeness era. But that doesn’t mean they’re immune to criticism.

Ahead of WSU’s next game, a road matchup with San Diego State, that brings up two key questions: How do these Cougars handle the noise? And without a bowl game to play for, what keeps them motivated?

“Regardless (of) what the prize is or whatever that we’re playing for, I want to win. I know all the guys in the locker room want to win, and the coaches want to win,” Leckner said. “So I think just the will to win. I think we have all the seniors, all the seniors that are still playing. We wanna send them out on a good note, and we wanna build momentum going into next year.”

This WSU team rosters 14 seniors, including key pieces like linebacker Keith Brown, offensive linemen Jonny Lester and Jaylin Caldwell, receivers Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons, defensive end Linus Zunk, defensive tackles Paul Hutson III and Damarjhe Lewis and tight end Jack Pedersen, plus cornerbacks Khamari Terrell and Jalil Tucker. All of those guys have played important roles for this team.

All three players who spoke to the media on Monday – Leckner, defensive end Matyus McLain and nickelback Jamarey Smith – agreed they’re motivated to keep playing for their seniors. They want to finish things right, especially for Brown, who is playing his sixth and final season of college football.

Fun fact about Brown: He’s played 482 snaps this season, which is the 12th most in the country among linebackers. It’s the third-most in the Pac-12. That underscores how reliable he has been this season, particularly in WSU’s last two games, making 15 tackles against Oregon State and nine against Boise State.

“Playing for the guys, playing for the seniors,” McLain said. “This is their last four games ever, could be ever. Playing for guys like Linus, Keith Brown. Gotta keep playing for those guys, and then just the guys in the locker room. You just gotta keep playing for everybody around you.”

Technically speaking, WSU isn’t entirely out of the bowl game picture. If they were to win out and end the regular season 5-7, they could make a bowl if there aren’t enough 6-6 teams to fill all the bowl slots. But the Cougars would also need to meet certain Academic Progress Rate standards, and they would need to decide if such a thing would benefit the program to begin with.

But that’s a long way off for WSU, which needs to beat an FBS team first before anything else can happen. The Cougars’ next task is a road tilt with the San Diego State Aztecs, who are favored to win the game, making the Cougars an underdog as they often have been this season.

“No offense to you guys, but you guys, the media people aren’t in our corner like our coaches are, and like we are for each other,” McLain said. “So really leaning on the brotherhood and the people in this building for the support that you need throughout that is really what it is.”

“I kinda block it out,” Smith said. “I worry about just what we have going on in the building and preparing week-by-week. Things that happened last week, to me, don’t really matter now. We’re on to San Diego State, bigger and better things. So just trying to prepare for that and dominate each and every week.”

Washington State.title: WSU's Darrius Clemons, Jeremiah Bernard day-to-day with injuries as Cougars play starters heavy snaps
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State may have to go another week without two starters on each side of the ball.

That’s according to head coach Kirby Moore, who said Monday that wide receiver Darrius Clemons (ankle) and safety Jeremiah Bernard (shoulder) are considered day-to-day ahead of a road matchup with San Diego State this Saturday. Both missed the Cougars’ home loss to Boise State last weekend, but both are set to return to practice this week, Moore added.

Their absences are wearing on a WSU team still looking for its first FBS win of the season, falling to 1-7 overall and 0-4 in Pac-12 play after a 31-10 home loss to BSU. Without Clemons, who suffered an ankle injury against Oregon State on Oct. 17, the Cougars didn’t expand their receiver rotation to include West Georgia transfer Jordan Dees or walk-on Caleb Northcroft, as Moore indicated could take place ahead of the game.

Instead, they played their top three receivers all heavy snaps: Branden Ganashamoorthy and Daniel Blood each played all 76 snaps of offense, while Tank Hawkins played 65 snaps. Those are the only three wideouts who played for Washington State in that game.

This season, Ganashamoorthy has played 503 snaps, the most among Pac-12 wide receivers. Four Cougars have played at least 500 snaps, making them one of only two Pac-12 teams to play four players that many snaps.

“We talk about deliberate practice,” Moore said. “That really starts with bringing great energy, having verbal combat, doing your assignment, making sure you’re not thinking out there, that you’re just reacting. I think we’ve had too many errors from a practice standpoint, with guys knowing their assignments, whether it’s motions, details within the position. We’ve got lot of trust in the guys who are out there on the field. If other guys improve and they’re to the standard, they’ll be out there.”

Bernard suffered his shoulder injury during WSU’s loss at Oregon State earlier this month, Moore said, describing it as “a little bit of a stinger.” In his absence, WSU coaches trusted Arizona State transfer Jackquintin Bal with 56 snaps, his second most of the season and his most in four games. Against Boise State, Bal wasn’t targeted in the secondary, but he missed four tackles, most on the team.

That contributed to the Cougars’ inability to prevent big plays on defense, like BSU star running back Dylan Riley’s touchdown rushes of 33 yards and 72 yards, both of which came during the Broncos’ 21-0 fourth quarter that they used to seal the win. As a team, WSU missed 16 tackles, bringing its season total to 93 – second most in the Pac-12, behind only Colorado State, which ranks last in the country in total defense.

Changes to O-line?

Moore said the team is “going to explore” shuffling personnel on its offensive line, which permitted 16 pressures and two sacks on QB Owen Eshelman against Boise State. The Cougars’ front five often allowed the Broncos to get home using stunts. Other times, that group was pushed back at the line of scrimmage, a big reason why running backs Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi managed only 20 yards on 10 carries.

As currently constructed, WSU’s starting offensive line includes right tackle Jaylin Caldwell, right guard Nick Bakken, center Noah Dunham, left guard Jonny Lester and left tackle Ashton Tripp, the last of whom returned to action last weekend after missing the Oregon State game with an ankle injury he sustained against Utah State on Oct. 9. All are returners, including Tripp and Lester, who started last season. Caldwell started two games before suffering an injury.

The possibilities seem numerous for the Cougars, who won’t be able to reach the six wins required for bowl eligibility, which the program has earned in 9 of the last 10 full seasons. Theoretically, WSU could still reach a bowl game by finishing the regular season 5-7, which would open up the possibility of being selected for a bowl if there aren’t enough 6-6 teams.

But the Cougs wouldn’t just end their five-game losing streak and win out. They would also need to achieve at least a 930 multiyear Academic Progress Rate.

“We’re gonna explore that this week with, obviously, practice,” Moore said of making changes on the offensive line. “We wanna give guys opportunities. At the same time, right now in the season, we gotta understand where we’re at, the communication with who’s been on the right side, with who’s been on the left side. Naturally, we wanna give some reps to some other guys as well, and then we gotta make a call there by the time we get to Thursday.”

Washington State.title: Still looking for first FBS win of season, WSU hits the road to take on San Diego State | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against San Diego State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

Looking to end a five-game slide and secure its first FBS win of the season, WSU heads to the Golden State to take on San Diego State, which has lost two of its last three games. The Cougars are coming off a 31-10 loss to Boise State, which marked quarterback Owen Eshelman’s second start.

It’s the first Pac-12 matchup between the Cougars and Aztecs, who have met each of the last two seasons, both wins for WSU. The Cougs, whose bye week comes next week, are also playing their third road game in the last four weeks.

Where is it?

Snapdragon Stadium in San Diego, California.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 4 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

CBS Sports Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

WSU opened as a 2.5-point underdog.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 31-10 loss to Boise State, WSU played the first-place Broncos to a 10-10 tie through three quarters, but that’s when things went south for the hosts. Boise State followed with a 21-0 fourth quarter, turning a costly Eshelman interception into a touchdown, then adding two more on each of its next two drives.

In Eshelman’s second start, it was another slow offensive outing for the Cougars, who tied the game shortly before halftime on a long touchdown drive and again on a field goal from kicker Jack Stevens, who has now connected on eight in a row. But that’s all the scoring WSU did, punting on four of its first five drives of the game.

The Cougars weren’t at full strength on offense. Wide receiver Darrius Clemons missed the game after going down the previous week with an ankle injury, a tough blow to a WSU receiver corps that has been thin since star wideout Tony Freeman tore his ACL in Week 1. But the Cougs didn’t exactly expand their rotation at that spot, instead opting to play receivers Branden Ganashamoorthy and Tank Hawkins heavy snaps and leaving Jordan Dees and Caleb Northcroft – both of whom WSU coach Kirby Moore said would get increased snaps – on the bench entirely.

Plus, the Cougars didn’t get much of anything from their rushing game, which produced only 53 yards on 33 carries. Running backs Kirby Vorhees and Leo Pulalasi accounted for only 20 yards on 10 carries, while fellow back Maxwell Woods played only 11 snaps and did not get any carries. In seven games against FBS competition, WSU running backs are averaging 15 carries for 48 yards.

That helped spotlight the problems facing WSU’s offensive line, which allowed 16 pressures and two sacks on Eshelman, who took four total. On several occasions, the Cougs were beaten on stunts. On others, they weren’t able to generate any push on running plays, a key reason why their running backs haven’t gotten anything consistent going. A group of five returners – left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell – have shared a good dosage of the blame for a paltry offense.

“Offensively, we weren’t good enough, especially up front,” Moore said, “protecting the quarterback, running the football, and it led to 17 third downs. We want to limit the number of third downs. We gotta be more efficient on first and second down and create more explosive plays.”

On defense, the Cougs allowed several more big plays, including two long touchdown rushes from Boise State star running back Dylan Riley, who piled up 128 yards and two touchdowns, both in the fourth quarter. WSU, which whiffed on 16 tackles, has had some issues preventing explosive plays all season.

Perhaps just as important: Washington State couldn’t generate any real pass rush. The Cougars finished with only eight pressures on QB Maddux Madsen, according to Pro Football Focus, which gave him ample time in the pocket to complete passes. Madsen completed several key third-down conversions, including a 17-yard scramble in the third quarter, which later led to a touchdown.

Scouting San Diego State …

In head coach Sean Lewis’ third season, the Aztecs are 3-5 overall and 2-2 in Pac-12 play, coming off a 56-49 road loss to Colorado State. In that one, backup QB Stone Saunders made his starting debut and threw two touchdowns against two interceptions, totaling 369 yards through the air.

But the Aztecs’ defense couldn’t make it count, as has been the case all season. After eight games, SDSU ranks No. 135 of 138 FBS teams in total defense (462 yards per game), No. 133 in scoring defense (36 points per game), No. 109 in rush defense (178 ypg) and No. 134 in pass defense (284 ypg). That group is also allowing opponents to convert third downs at a 47% clip, which is No. 129 nationally.

It hasn’t been pretty for SDSU’s defense, which had to replace several key pieces on last year’s unit, including cornerback Chris Johnson, a first-round NFL draft pick in the spring, as well as edge rusher Trey White and three others who transferred to Power Four schools.

The Aztecs are dealing with an injury to quarterback Jayden Denegal, the team’s starter for the first seven games. The Aztecs opened the season with a home romp over FCS Portland State, only to drop three straight games, including road matchups with UCLA and Toledo and a home contest against James Madison. Since then, SDSU has dispatched Texas State at home, lost to Oregon State on the road, bounced back with a home win over Fresno State then fell in a road tilt with CSU.

In the Aztecs’ win over the Bulldogs, Saunders came on for the injured Denegal, leading fourth-quarter two scoring drives to secure the win. Listed at 6-foot-1 and 222 pounds, Saunders profiles as a pure pocket-passer, and he does it well. In his first start last weekend, Saunders completed 23 of 33 passes for 369 yards, two touchdowns and two picks. He isn’t much of a mobile threat, posting only four carries for minus-9 yards, an indication of the two total sacks he’s taken.

“They’re doing a nice job of playing complementary football,” Moore said. “They got in a shootout last week. They’re 3-1 at home. For us, it’s gonna be a challenge, third out of four games being on the road.”

What happened last time?

WSU and San Diego State’s last meeting came last fall in Pullman, where former Cougar quarterback Jaxon Potter led his team to a 36-13 win, scoring 22 unanswered points to pull away. Potter would go on to make one more start, in a loss to North Texas, before being benched for veteran Zevi Eckhaus for the rest of the season.

Washington State.title: 2027 Apple Cup moved up three weeks to Aug. 28
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The 2027 Apple Cup will be played in August.

Washington State and Washington have agreed to move next year’s rivalry game from Sept. 18 to Aug. 28, according to a Monday release, moving the longstanding series to August for the first time in its 118-year history.

The 2027 game, set for Gesa Field in Pullman, will be the fourth game of a five-year series extension the sides agreed to in 2023, not long after the traditional Pac-12’s collapse. The 2028 game, scheduled for Seattle, is the last one under contract.

The Huskies won this year’s game, a 24-10 decision in Seattle, and they own an all-time advantage of 78-34-6.

With this move, WSU now has a bye for its fourth week of action. Here is the Cougars’ 2027 schedule so far.

Aug. 28: vs. Washington

Sept. 4: vs. Idaho

Sept. 11: vs. Kansas

Sept. 18: Idle

Sept. 25: at Arizona

Washington State.title: As chaos reigns and CFP rankings loom, Boise State and Oregon State remain on track | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

The Pac-12 dodged the mayhem that walloped conferences across the country the past two weekends.

As undefeated teams tumbled and title favorites flopped, Boise State and Oregon State held their positions as the frontrunners for the Pac-12 championship and a potential berth in the College Football Playoff.

One Saturday remains before the first CFP rankings are released Nov. 3. If the Broncos handle Texas State at home and the Beavers win at Fresno State – it’s their toughest assignment since conference play began – at least one, if not both, will receive consideration for a spot in the selection committee’s top 25.

For the moment, UT-San Antonio, from the American, is the highest-ranked team in ESPN’s strength-of-record (SOR), an important data point that mirrors the private version used by the selection committee.

SOR measures how a given team performs against its schedule compared to how an average Top 25 team would fare against the same schedule. It offers the committee a means of comparing teams with similar records but no head-to-head results.

UTSA is ranked 23rd in the SOR metric, one spot ahead of Boise State. The Roadrunners have one loss: by 24 points at Texas, while the Broncos’ lone defeat was by seven points at Oregon. The teams’ strength-of-schedule rankings are comparable.

(Notably, UTSA’s toughest remaining game, against North Texas, is the same day, Nov. 14, as the Boise State-Oregon State showdown.)

Only No. 34 New Mexico, the Mountain West frontrunner, and No. 39 James Madison, from the Sun Belt, are close to UTSA and Boise State in the SOR rankings.

Then comes No. 45 Louisiana Tech (Sun Belt), No. 47 North Texas (American) and No. 49 Liberty (Conference USA).

The Beavers are 50th, which reflects their weak collection of victories. Of course, that will change if they defeat Fresno State, Texas State and Boise State in the upcoming triple whammy.

Which scenario would best position the Pac-12 for the berth in the CFP reserved for the top team in the Group of Six?

It’s possible the conference would be well served by Oregon State winning out and Boise State losing only to the Beavers.

That would result in a matchup of 10-2 teams for the conference title, placing the winner, whether it’s the Broncos or Beavers, in prime position for the playoff bid.

Granted, the results in the American and Mountain West in coming weeks will shape the Group of Six landscape.

But given the lunacy across the country – not to mention the plot twist currently unfolding 45 miles south of Corvallis – the Pac-12 should consider itself fortunate.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (6-1/3-0)

Result: won at Washington State 31-10

Next up: vs. Texas State (7 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: Remember back in September, when we described the result at Oregon as a quality loss that would strengthen the Broncos’ resume in much the same fashion as the narrow defeat in Eugene in 2024? Never mind. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (5-2/3-0)

Result: did not play

Next up: at Fresno State (8 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Texas Tech and Houston did Oregon State no favors Saturday with their losses. If the Beavers end up in a resume showdown for a playoff berth with the best team in the American or Mountain West, they would benefit from claiming a close defeat to a Big 12 playoff-bound team. That scenario is less likely than it was a few days ago. (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (4-3/1-2)

Result: did not play

Next up: vs. Oregon State (8 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: The Bulldogs’ pass defense is statistically average compared to the other 137 FBS teams. There is nothing average about Oregon State’s aerial attack. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (3-4/1-2)

Result: beat San Diego State 56-49

Next up: at Utah State (12:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: As insane as it sounds, holding their opponent to 49 points constitutes an improvement for the Rams, who have allowed at least 56 points in each of the previous three games. (Last week: 6)

5. San Diego State (3-5/2-2)

Result: lost at Colorado State 56-49

Next up: vs. Washington State (4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: That was a bad loss for SDSU’s bowl math. A very bad loss. Now, the Aztecs must handle Washington State and Utah State at home and either beat Boise State or win their Flex Saturday matchup, which will be on the road. (Last week: 4)

6. Texas State (4-3/2-1)

Result: beat Utah State 20-17

Next up: at Boise State (7 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: With Boise State and Oregon State on the road on consecutive Saturdays, the Bobcats should stay in Bend for the week rather than schlepping home and back. They will be far better prepared for whatever weather awaits them in Corvallis. (We’re joking, mostly.) (Last week: 5)

7. Utah State (2-5/1-2)

Result: lost at Texas State 20-17

Next up: vs. Colorado State (12:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: There goes Bronco Mendenhall, nearly pulling off a Bronco Mendenhall? Oh well, there will be more opportunities for the Aggies to rise up and disrupt the race in November. (Last week: 7)

8. Washington State (1-7/0-4)

Result: lost to Boise State 31-10

Next up: at San Diego State (4 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: Given the level of competition in the new Pac-12, which is substantially worse than in the old Pac-12, this qualifies as one of the most disappointing seasons in the modern history of WSU football. There are problems galore, and coach Kirby Moore seemingly has no answers. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: An uncertain future for an Apple Cup hoops rivalry that only one side wants to preserve
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – The hoops version of the Apple Cup is unrecognizable these days.

Washington and Washington State have been playing against each other since 1910 and have matched up in 301 games, which is one of the oldest and most played series in men’s college basketball.

In front of 7,011 fans at Alaska Airlines Arena, the two teams met once again Sunday afternoon, and the Huskies lost 84-80 in an exhibition in a rivalry that used to mean something.

“Rivalries in college basketball, it’s tough,” said former UW star Isaiah Thomas who watched from stands below his No. 2 jersey, which hangs in the rafters. “It’s a different time, day and age.”

The 37-year-old Thomas talked to the Huskies before the game and tried to explain the importance of the UW-WSU rivalry to a team comprised of 12 newcomers born outside of the state, including five international players.

“It’s just human nature if you’re not from here to be a little clueless about the Apple Cup and what that really means,” Thomas said. “All these games probably feel the same, but just reminding them that it’s not about you the individual. It’s about the program, the city and the state rivalry.

“You just understand it more and more the longer you’re here. My job is to show them that it does mean something no matter if it’s a game that counts or not.”

Did they receive the message?

“If we win, they did,” Thomas said smiling at halftime. “If we lose, they didn’t.”

None of the current Cougars played in last year’s 81-69 loss while Wesley Yates III, Lathan Sommerville and Jasir Rencher suited up for the Huskies.

“I’ve coached two of their guys more than either of us have coached an entire team,” WSU coach David Riley said referring to UW’s Steele Venters and LeJuan Watts. “It’s a weird deal.”

Riley coached Venters at Eastern Washington and led Watts at EWU and at WSU.

“This is always a fun game, but I’ve never won so maybe it’s me,” Watts said smiling, referring to his 0-2 Apple Cup record, including an 89-73 WSU loss on Dec. 18, 2024, when he tallied 15 point, eight rebounds and three assists. “There’s no little brother thing (at Washington). That’s kind of what it was on the other side, just being the underdog.

“It’s a lot more drive and motivation if you’re Wazzu. I mean, you don’t have anything to lose.”

Despite a game-high 28 points on 7-for-12 shooting from the field from Watts, Lathan Sommerville scoring 19 points and Nikola Dzepina adding 16 points and 12 rebounds, Washington lost control midway in the second half.

The Huskies led 50-43 when the Cougars took control for good with a 13-2 run to go up 56-52 following an alley-oop dunk from Ronnie Harrison, who finished with a team-high 23 points.

Washington State went up 79-71 with 46 seconds left when Washington made one last push and cut its deficit to 81-78 following Venters’ 3-pointer with 15 seconds left.

After WSU guard Casey Jones missed a couple of free throws, the Huskies had a chance to tie but Watts’ 3-point attempt was deflected and fell short.

When it was over, Riley admitted he’s not sure if the series will continue.

“I hope we can get them on the schedule for a real game next year,” he said. “We’re taking this thing day by day. There’s a lot going on. There’s a lot of changes in college basketball, so hopefully we can make it happen next year.”

The Cougars have ceded the fate of the Apple Cup to the Huskies because they’re struggling to remain financially viable even in the Pac-12.

Among its 16 nonconference matchups on the 2026-27 schedule, Washington State plays just five in Pullman and nine on the road against High Point, Duquesne, Hawaii, Duke, Murray State, Southern Illinois, Weber State, UNLV, Seattle U, Eastern Washington and LSU.

“Home games against lesser teams usually cost a lot of money, and we’re in a spot now where it’s like we’d rather spend some of that on our roster,” Riley said. “We’re in a tough spot. It’s hard to find home-and-home (deals), especially in Pullman. So, we’re going on the road a lot and that’s part of the deal where we’re just, we’re going to play anyone anywhere at any time. We have a hard schedule, and we’ll be hardened by the time conference play hits.”

UW coach Danny Sprinkle, who begins his third season with the Huskies, knows canceling series with traditional rivals Gonzaga, Seattle U and potentially Washington State, is unpopular with UW fans.

However, he has his reasons.

“I know I’ll get killed for not playing (the Cougars) this year, but with our schedule, I have to do what’s best for Washington basketball,” Sprinkle said. “Fitting them in at a certain time, it was hard with us going to the Maui and playing BYU and two other terrific teams. Already having Baylor coming here, going to Utah, and then a lot of people around here forget you’re playing 20 Big Ten games … and probably 18 of them are Quad 1 games against the hardest teams in the country. So, that takes a toll on you.”

Riley, who is close friends with Sprinkle, understands.

“I’ve known Danny a long time,” he said. “There’s only a couple friends I’ve got in this business and he’s one of them. … He’s a good coach, great guy and he has to do what’s best for his team.”

Still, he wants the Apple Cup to continue.

“Whatever they tell us, we’ll go play the game,” Riley said. “We’ll find a way to make it work because it’s important to me. It’s important to our fans. It’s a great game, and it’s worth preserving.”

PAC-12 CHAOS! Colorado State Wins 56–49, Boise State Rolls WSU | Pac Pulse Week 8
Washington State.summary:
Week 8 delivered plenty of Pac-12 chaos.

Washington State.title: Washington State beats rival Washington in men's basketball exhibition
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – For the first time since 1917, the men’s basketball teams from Washington State and Washington won’t meet in the regular season. But the Cougars still got a shot at their bitter rivals in a preseason matchup, and made the most of it.

WSU topped UW 84-80 in an exhibition on Sunday at Alaska Airlines Arena – a preseason boost for a Cougars team that was coming off a 28-point exhibition loss at New Mexico on Oct. 18.

The 7,011 in attendance were treated to a free-throw shootout. The teams combined for 87 foul shots. WSU went 31 of 46 from the line and the Huskies shot 30 of 41 from the stripe. The teams both shot 22 of 56 from the field. WSU’s 9-for-26 mark from 3-point range – compared to UW’s 6-for-23 – gave the visitors the edge.

The Cougars trailed by 10 points midway through the first half, but used an 8-2 run to get back in it and took a 38-37 lead into halftime. The Huskies opened a seven-point lead about seven minutes into the second period before a Casey Jones 3 keyed a 13-2 WSU run that put the Cougars up by four.

WSU’s Ronnie Harrison scored back-to-back buckets on a tip-in and a dunk with just over five minutes left to break a tie. The Cougars led by as many as eight points with under a minute left before a UW rally, but WSU got a game-winning block from Harrison on LeJuan Watts’ game-tying 3-point attempt with six seconds left.

Harrison, a senior transfer forward from East Texas A&M, led the Cougs with 23 points and 11 rebounds, shooting 8 of 9 from the floor. Guard Lazerek Houston, a Central Missouri transfer, added 15 points. Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips chipped in 12 points. Providence transfer guard Jaylen Harrell scored 11 points and Jones, a former Eastern Washington standout, had 10 for the new-look Cougars, who had to entirely rebuild their roster this offseason.

Watts, a former WSU and EWU star who spent last season at Texas Tech, led the Huskies with 28 points, shooting 7 of 12 from the field and 12 of 13 from the foul line. Gonzaga transfer Steele Venters had three points for UW.

The Cougs open their regular season Nov. 2 at home against Davidson.
